name: Portuguese colonization of Brazil
summary: Portugal claimed Brazil in 1500 and settled it over the following three centuries, building a colony on brazilwood, sugar, gold and the labour of enslaved Africans. It became the largest and most valuable possession of the Portuguese empire, and the only Portuguese-speaking country in the Americas.
body:
Part of [Age of Discovery](event:age-of-discovery). Pedro Álvares Cabral made landfall on the coast in April 1500 while sailing for India. The crown at first neglected the territory, since the [spice trade](event:da-gama) promised more, and the first export was brazilwood, a red dyewood that gave the country its name. Permanent settlement began in the 1530s with hereditary captaincies granted to noblemen, and a governor-general was installed at Salvador in 1549.

Sugar plantations in the north-east made the colony profitable from the later sixteenth century, worked first by Indigenous people and then, in far greater numbers, by [enslaved Africans](event:slave-trade); Brazil received more captives than any other destination in the Americas. Bandeirante expeditions out of São Paulo pushed the frontier far west of the line agreed at Tordesillas, and the discovery of gold in Minas Gerais in the 1690s shifted the colony's centre south, which is why the capital moved to Rio de Janeiro in 1763.

By 1800 Brazil was worth more to Lisbon than everything else it held. Portuguese, Indigenous and African populations mixed to a degree unlike the mainland. When the royal court fled Napoleon's armies for Rio in 1807 the colony briefly became the seat of the empire — a reversal that led to independence in 1822.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colonial_Brazil).

name: Swahili city-states and Indian Ocean trade
summary: A chain of Muslim merchant cities along the East African coast, from Mogadishu to Kilwa and Sofala, traded gold, ivory and enslaved people into the Indian Ocean world. Their language and culture, Swahili, blended African, Arab and Persian elements.
body:
The Swahili towns were African cities of coral stone, ruled by their own sultans and merchant families and tied by the monsoon to Arabia, Persia, Gujarat and, at a remove, China. Gold from the Zimbabwe plateau reached the sea at Sofala and Kilwa; ivory, timber and captives went out, and cotton cloth, beads and porcelain came in.

Portuguese fleets bombarded and occupied several towns after 1500 and built Fort Jesus at Mombasa in 1593, trying to tax and redirect the trade. They never controlled it. Arab, Gujarati and Swahili merchants went on sailing, and in 1698 Omani forces took Mombasa and pushed the Portuguese south of Cape Delgado. Zanzibar became the leading port under Omani rule in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, and the centre of a clove economy and an expanded slave trade into the interior.

Swahili is a Bantu language carrying heavy Arabic and Persian borrowing — the linguistic trace of that commerce. It is now spoken by over a hundred million people and is an official language of Kenya, Tanzania, Uganda and the African Union.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swahili_city-states).

name: Safavid Empire at its height
summary: The Safavid dynasty ruled Iran from 1501 to 1736, made Twelver Shia Islam the state religion, and fought the Sunni Ottomans for two centuries over the western frontier. Their capital at Isfahan was one of the great cities of the seventeenth century.
body:
Ismail I took Tabriz in 1501 at about fourteen and proclaimed Shia Islam the religion of his realm, converting a largely Sunni population by force and patronage over the following century — the decision that fixed Iran's religious identity to the present day. Defeat by Ottoman firearms at Chaldiran in 1514 set the pattern of a long war in Mesopotamia and the Caucasus that neither side could win outright.

Abbas I, who ruled from 1588 to 1629, rebuilt the army around gunpowder and slave regiments drawn from the Caucasus, recovered lost provinces, and moved the capital to Isfahan, where he laid out the Naqsh-e Jahan square with its mosques, palace and bazaar. Persian carpets, silk, miniature painting and calligraphy found buyers as far as Europe, and English and Dutch companies traded through the Gulf.

The state weakened under his successors. In 1722 an Afghan army sacked Isfahan; Nader Shah drove the invaders out and ruled in the dynasty's name before taking the throne himself, and the Safavid line formally ended in 1736. Its religious settlement and its court culture outlasted it by centuries.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Safavid_Empire).

name: Leonardo paints the Mona Lisa
summary: Leonardo da Vinci's small oil portrait of Lisa Gherardini, begun in Florence in about 1503, is the best-known painting in the world. It has hung in the Louvre in Paris since the 1790s.
body:
Part of [The Renaissance](event:renaissance). The panel is oil on poplar and measures 77 by 53 centimetres. The sitter is generally identified as Lisa Gherardini, wife of the Florentine silk merchant Francesco del Giocondo — hence the Italian title *La Gioconda*. [Leonardo](item:leonardo-da-vinci) seems to have kept working on it for years and never delivered it; he carried it to France, where Francis I acquired it.

Two things account for the technique's reputation. Sfumato is the smoke-like blending of tone that leaves no drawn line at the edges of the face, so that the expression appears to shift with the angle of viewing. Behind the sitter an imaginary landscape of water and crags recedes into blue haze, with the horizon set slightly higher on one side than the other.

The painting was admired by artists long before it was famous generally; its worldwide celebrity dates from its theft from the Louvre in 1911 by Vincenzo Peruggia, an Italian workman who wanted it returned to Italy, and its recovery two years later. It is now shown behind glass and is the most visited object in any museum.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mona_Lisa).

name: Michelangelo paints the Sistine Chapel
summary: Michelangelo painted the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel in the Vatican between 1508 and 1512, on a commission from Pope Julius II. Its nine scenes from Genesis, among them the Creation of Adam, are the most reproduced images in Western art.
body:
Part of [The Renaissance](event:renaissance). Michelangelo thought of himself as a sculptor and took the commission reluctantly, having wanted to carry on with the pope's tomb. He designed his own scaffolding, bridged from holes in the walls rather than built up from the floor, and worked in true fresco — pigment laid into wet plaster, which must be finished before the day's patch dries and cannot easily be corrected. He stood to paint, head back; he did not lie down, though he complained in a verse letter that the work was ruining his neck.

The scheme covers about 500 square metres. Nine Genesis scenes run down the centre, from the separation of light and darkness to the drunkenness of Noah, framed by painted architecture and surrounded by prophets, sibyls and the ancestors of Christ. The figures grow larger and more freely handled towards the altar end, which is the direction in which the work proceeded.

He returned decades later, from 1536 to 1541, to paint The Last Judgement on the altar wall. A cleaning finished in 1994 removed centuries of candle soot and glue and revealed colours far brighter than the ones generations had known, which was itself much argued over.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sistine_Chapel_ceiling).

name: Portuguese conquest of Goa
summary: Afonso de Albuquerque took the port of Goa from the Sultanate of Bijapur in 1510. It became the capital of the Portuguese State of India and the hub of Portuguese power in Asia for four and a half centuries.
body:
Part of [Age of Discovery](event:age-of-discovery). Albuquerque seized the city in March 1510, was driven out in May, and retook it on 25 November with a larger fleet. He chose it for its sheltered harbour, its position on the Konkan coast between the pepper ports and the Arabian Sea, and its usefulness as a base against the Muslim shipping that had carried the spice trade to Egypt.

Goa became the seat of a viceroy, an archbishopric, and from 1560 an Inquisition. Portuguese strategy in Asia depended less on territory than on a chain of fortified harbours — Hormuz, Malacca, Colombo, Macau — and on the *cartaz*, a licence that armed carracks enforced against any ship trading without one. Small garrisons held the chain because shipboard gunnery outmatched what the local powers put afloat, and because Portugal made alliances with rulers who had their own reasons to want the incumbents weakened.

The city declined after the seventeenth century as Dutch and English competitors took the trade, and the administration moved to Panjim in the 1840s. Portuguese Goa outlasted the empire that made it: it was annexed by India in 1961, after 451 years.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_conquest_of_Goa).

name: Bartolomé de las Casas advocates for Indigenous peoples
summary: Bartolomé de las Casas, a Spanish colonist who became a Dominican friar, spent fifty years arguing that the Indigenous peoples of the Americas were fully human, held rights, and could not lawfully be enslaved or conquered.
body:
Las Casas came to Hispaniola as a young man and held an *encomienda* — a grant of Indigenous labour — before renouncing it in 1514 and taking orders. He crossed the Atlantic repeatedly to press his case at court, and his *A Short Account of the Destruction of the Indies*, published in 1552, catalogued the violence of the [conquest](event:spanish-conquest) in detail meant to force the Crown to act.

His arguments contributed to the New Laws of 1542, which restricted the encomienda and forbade Indigenous slavery; colonial resistance was fierce enough that key clauses were repealed within three years. In 1550 and 1551 he debated Juan Ginés de Sepúlveda before a royal junta at Valladolid, who held that the Indigenous were natural slaves whom Spain might justly subdue. No verdict was pronounced, but the question had been put in terms of law and conscience rather than of conquest.

He is not a simple figure. He early proposed importing enslaved Africans to spare Indigenous labourers, and later repudiated the proposal as the same wrong. His writing was translated across Protestant Europe and used as anti-Spanish propaganda. It remains one of the founding texts of the argument that colonised peoples hold rights that a conqueror may not cancel.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bartolomé_de_las_Casas).

name: Protestant Reformation
summary: The Reformation split Western Christianity. From Martin Luther's protest against indulgences in 1517, reformers rejected papal authority and much of Catholic doctrine, and within a generation much of northern Europe had left the Roman church. The division reshaped politics as much as religion, and the wars it fed ran on until 1648.
body:
Much of the criticism was old: clerical wealth, absentee bishops, the sale of pardons and the papacy's temporal power had been attacked for two centuries. What was new was reach. The [printing press](event:printing-press) carried Luther's tracts across Germany in weeks, vernacular Bibles put the text in lay hands, and princes who wanted church lands and independence from the emperor had reasons of their own to protect him.

It was never one movement. Luther held to a real presence in the Eucharist that Zwingli denied, and the two failed to agree at Marburg in 1529. Anabaptists rejected infant baptism and were persecuted by Catholics and Protestants alike. Calvin's Geneva produced a disciplined church order that spread to France, Scotland, the Netherlands and the Rhine. England's break was made by a king for dynastic reasons and given a Protestant content afterwards. Catholic reform answered at the Council of Trent, which restated doctrine without concession and tightened clerical discipline, and in new orders, above all the Jesuits.

The settlement was fought over for a century and a quarter — in Germany, in the French wars of religion, in the [Dutch Revolt](event:netherlands-independence), and finally in the [Thirty Years' War](event:thirty-years-war). The [Peace of Westphalia](event:westphalia) of 1648 ended the fighting by conceding that Europe would stay divided. It left the sovereign state, rather than a universal church, as the thing that decided such questions — along with mass literacy, national vernaculars and a confessional map of Europe still visible today.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reformation).

steps.name: The Diet of Worms
steps.page:
Summoned before Charles V and the imperial diet at Worms in April 1521, Luther was shown his books and asked to retract them. He refused unless convinced by scripture or plain reason, and was given safe conduct home.

The Edict of Worms in May declared him an outlaw whom anyone might kill without penalty, and banned his writings. The Elector of Saxony had him taken to the Wartburg instead, where he translated the New Testament into German.

steps.name: The German Peasants' War
steps.page:
Peasants and townsmen across southern and central Germany rose from 1524, citing the gospel against serfdom, tithes and hunting rights; the Twelve Articles of Memmingen were among the first printed statements of popular grievance in Europe.

Luther, whose language they had borrowed, denounced them and urged the princes to strike. Perhaps 100,000 were killed. The reformation of the church was decisively attached to the authority of the princes rather than to the commons.

steps.name: The Augsburg Confession
steps.page:
Melanchthon's statement of Lutheran doctrine was read to the emperor at the diet of Augsburg in June 1530. It was drafted to look as little heretical as possible, and it remains the confessional basis of Lutheran churches.

Rejected by the Catholic side, it hardened the division into two organised parties and led directly to the defensive Schmalkaldic League of Protestant princes.

steps.name: Calvin's Geneva
steps.page:
John Calvin returned to Geneva in 1541 and built a church order of pastors, teachers, elders and deacons, with a consistory that supervised belief and conduct. His *Institutes of the Christian Religion*, revised through his life, became the most systematic statement of Reformed theology.

The city took in refugees and printed for export. Reformed churches on the Genevan model spread to France, Scotland, the Netherlands and the Rhineland — the branch of the Reformation that travelled furthest.

name: Luther's Ninety-five Theses
summary: On 31 October 1517 Martin Luther, a friar and professor at Wittenberg, sent his archbishop ninety-five propositions attacking the sale of indulgences. Printed and circulated within weeks, they became the opening of the Reformation.
body:
Part of [Protestant Reformation](event:reformation). An indulgence remitted temporal punishment for sin. The campaign Luther objected to was being preached near Saxony by Johann Tetzel, to help pay for the rebuilding of St Peter's in Rome and to clear the debts Albert of Mainz had run up buying his archbishopric. Luther's theses argued that the pope could not remit guilt, that a truly penitent Christian already has forgiveness without a letter, and that the money would be better given to the poor.

They were written in Latin, for academic disputation, and sent to Albert with a covering letter. Within two months they had been translated into German, printed and read across the empire, at a speed the [printing press](event:printing-press) made possible and which nobody involved had planned for. The story that Luther nailed them to the door of the Castle Church is first told after his death and is disputed by historians.

Rome treated the affair as a quarrel among friars until it was too late. Luther refused to recant before the emperor at Worms in 1521 and was excommunicated and outlawed; sheltered at the Wartburg by the Elector of Saxony, he translated the New Testament into German in eleven weeks. A dispute over a fundraising practice had become a break with the papacy.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ninety-five_Theses).

name: First circumnavigation of the globe
summary: A Spanish expedition under Ferdinand Magellan left Sanlúcar in September 1519 to reach the Spice Islands by sailing west. Magellan was killed in the Philippines, but one ship, the Victoria, came home in 1522 under Juan Sebastián Elcano — the first voyage around the world.
body:
Part of [Age of Discovery](event:age-of-discovery). Magellan was Portuguese and sailed for Castile after his own king refused him. Five ships and about 270 men set out to find a passage through the Americas to the ocean Balboa had sighted in 1513, and so to reach the Moluccas westward — which, under the Treaty of Tordesillas, would put the spice trade in Spanish hands.

The voyage cost four ships and most of the crew. One was wrecked on the Patagonian coast, one deserted in the strait and sailed home, one was left in the Moluccas as unseaworthy, and Magellan himself was killed at Mactan in April 1521 in a fight he had entered on behalf of a local ally he had converted. The Pacific crossing took ninety-eight days without fresh food; the survivors ate leather stripped from the yards and sawdust, and scurvy killed about twenty men.

Eighteen men reached Sanlúcar aboard the Victoria on 6 September 1522, with a cargo of cloves that covered the cost of the whole expedition. They had shown the oceans to be continuous and the world far larger than Columbus had reckoned — and they found their carefully kept log a day behind the calendar ashore, the first practical encounter with what the international date line now settles.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magellan_expedition).

steps.name: Departure from Sanlúcar
steps.page:
Five ships — Trinidad, San Antonio, Concepción, Victoria and Santiago — and about 270 men left Sanlúcar de Barrameda on 20 September 1519, having dropped down from Seville the month before.

The Spanish captains resented serving a Portuguese commander from the start, and Magellan kept his intended route to himself.

steps.name: Wintering and mutiny at San Julián
steps.page:
The fleet put into Port St Julian on the Patagonian coast on 31 March 1520 to wait out the southern winter. Three captains mutinied within days; Magellan recovered control, had one killed and another executed, and marooned two men on the shore.

The Santiago was wrecked while scouting south. The fleet stayed five months, and it was here that the Europeans met the tall Tehuelche people whom Magellan's chronicler called Patagons.

steps.name: Through the strait
steps.page:
A headland sighted on 21 October opened into a channel that ran west for 570 kilometres between cliffs and glaciers. It took thirty-eight days to work through, with boats sent ahead to find which of the branching passages led on.

The San Antonio, the largest ship and the one carrying most of the provisions, turned back for Spain during the search. Three ships came out into the open ocean on 28 November, which Magellan named the Pacific for its calm.

steps.name: Ninety-eight days across the Pacific
steps.page:
Nobody knew how wide the ocean was, and the crossing took over three months without sight of an inhabited island. The biscuit turned to powder and maggots, the water stank, and the men ate sawdust and ox hides soaked and grilled.

Scurvy killed about twenty men and disabled most of the rest. They made landfall at Guam on 6 March 1521.

steps.name: The Philippines and Magellan's death
steps.page:
The fleet reached Samar on 16 March 1521 and made an alliance at Cebu, where the ruler and hundreds of his people accepted baptism. Magellan then agreed to subdue a neighbouring chief, Lapu-Lapu of Mactan, who had refused to submit.

He landed with about fifty men on 27 April, kept the ships' guns out of range, and was killed in the shallows. Survivors were massacred at a banquet at Cebu days later, and the Concepción was burned for want of crew.

steps.name: The Moluccas
steps.page:
The two remaining ships reached Tidore in the Moluccas on 8 November 1521 and loaded cloves — the cargo the whole venture had been mounted for, and worth more than the fleet.

The Trinidad was found to be leaking and stayed behind to be repaired; she later tried to recross the Pacific eastward, failed, and was taken by the Portuguese. Only the Victoria sailed for home, under Juan Sebastián Elcano.

steps.name: The Victoria comes home
steps.page:
Elcano took the Victoria west across the Indian Ocean and round the Cape, avoiding Portuguese ports, and reached Sanlúcar on 6 September 1522 with eighteen men aboard and the ship barely afloat.

The cloves in her hold covered the cost of the expedition. Comparing their log with the calendar ashore, the survivors found they had lost a day — the first practical encounter with what the international date line now settles.

name: Spanish conquest of the Americas
summary: Between 1519 and 1572 Spanish expeditions overthrew the Aztec and Inca empires and claimed most of the Americas for the crown of Castile. Small Spanish forces succeeded through firearms, horses and steel, through alliances with peoples subject to those empires, and through epidemic disease that had arrived ahead of them.
body:
Conquest was carried out by licensed private ventures rather than royal armies: a leader raised men and money on credit and was paid in a share of the loot and in *encomiendas*, grants of Indigenous labour. Hernán Cortés landed in Mexico in 1519 with about 500 men and took [Tenochtitlan](event:tenochtitlan) in 1521 with tens of thousands of Tlaxcalan allies. Francisco Pizarro seized the Inca emperor Atahualpa in 1532, at a moment when the [Inca](event:inca-conquest) were emerging from a war of succession between two brothers, and held Cusco by the end of 1533.

Neither conquest was quick or complete. Maya polities in Yucatán and Guatemala resisted for decades, and the last independent one, Nojpetén, fell only in 1697; a rump Inca state held out at Vilcabamba until 1572; the Mapuche of southern Chile were never subdued. Rebellion and the collapse of the Indigenous population made the conquered lands hard to hold and harder to tax.

What replaced the old empires was a colonial order of viceroyalties, Catholic missions, cathedral cities and silver mines. Bullion from [Potosí](event:potosi-silver) and Zacatecas financed Habsburg Spain and reached China aboard the [Manila galleons](event:manila-galleon). The crown legislated repeatedly against the worst abuses under pressure from clerics such as [Las Casas](event:las-casas), with limited effect at the distance involved.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_colonization_of_the_Americas).

steps.name: Cortés lands in Mexico
steps.page:
Hernán Cortés landed near modern Veracruz in April 1519 with about 500 men, sixteen horses and a few guns, in defiance of the governor of Cuba who had tried to recall him. He founded a town, had it elect him, and so claimed to answer to the king alone.

He beached his ships to stop anyone returning, and marched inland gathering allies among the Totonacs and then the Tlaxcalans, who fought him hard before joining him.

steps.name: The Maya campaigns
steps.page:
Pedro de Alvarado moved into Guatemala in 1524 and Francisco de Montejo into Yucatán from 1527. Neither found a single capital to capture: Maya political power was divided among many kingdoms, in country that suited defenders.

Yucatán took nearly twenty years and two abandoned attempts before Mérida was founded in 1542 and the north subdued by 1546. The last independent Maya state, Nojpetén in the Petén lakes, held out until 1697.

steps.name: The New Laws
steps.page:
Pressed by [Las Casas](event:las-casas) and by the Council of the Indies, Charles V issued laws in November 1542 forbidding the enslavement of Indigenous people, limiting the *encomienda* and ending its inheritance.

The colonists rebelled. A viceroy sent to enforce the laws in Peru was defeated and beheaded in 1546, and the inheritance clause was repealed. The crown had asserted that the conquered were its subjects rather than the conquerors' property, and had shown how little it could enforce at that distance.

steps.name: The last Inca state falls
steps.page:
A rump Inca state had survived since 1537 in the forested mountains at Vilcabamba, north-west of Cusco, under Manco Inca and his sons. It raided the highways and sheltered those who would not submit.

Viceroy Toledo sent an expedition in 1572. Vilcabamba was burned, and the last Inca, Túpac Amaru, was brought to Cusco and beheaded in the square before a crowd that is said to have begged for his life. Toledo's reorganisation of labour and settlement followed.

name: Epidemics devastate the Americas
summary: Old World diseases reached the Americas with Europeans and killed most of the Indigenous population within a century. Smallpox, measles, typhus and unidentified fevers often spread far ahead of settlers. Estimates of the overall decline run from about 80 to 95 per cent, and they vary widely because the pre-contact population is itself disputed.
body:
Part of [The Columbian Exchange](event:columbian-exchange). Populations separated from Eurasia and Africa for thousands of years had no acquired immunity to smallpox, measles, influenza, typhus or malaria, and the diseases arrived together rather than one at a time, so that a society weakened by one outbreak met the next before it had recovered. Epidemics moved along Indigenous trade and tribute routes, which meant that many peoples were struck before they had seen a European at all.

Disease was not the whole of it. War, enslavement, forced labour in mines and fields, the seizure of stored food, the disruption of planting and the breakdown of households with nobody well enough to fetch water made each outbreak far deadlier than the pathogen alone would have been. In most regions the population did not begin to recover until the eighteenth century.

The scale of the depopulation may even be readable in the atmosphere: one much-discussed study argues that forest regrowing on abandoned farmland drew down enough carbon dioxide to register in Antarctic ice cores around 1610. Arguments of that kind depend on pre-contact population figures that specialists still dispute by a factor of several.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Population_history_of_Indigenous_peoples_of_the_Americas).

steps.name: Smallpox reaches Mexico
steps.page:
Smallpox came ashore with a Spanish expedition in 1520 and reached the Valley of Mexico while the war with Cortés was under way. It killed the emperor Cuitláhuac and a large share of the population of [Tenochtitlan](event:tenochtitlan) during the siege.

From there it spread through Mesoamerica along established trade and tribute routes, reaching Guatemala by 1521, where the Kaqchikel annals record it independently of any European presence.

steps.name: Smallpox in the Andes
steps.page:
The epidemic ran ahead of the Spanish down the Andes and reached the Inca empire several years before Pizarro did. It killed the emperor Huayna Capac and his designated heir.

The succession war between Atahualpa and Huáscar that followed is what left the empire divided when the [Spanish arrived](event:inca-conquest) in 1532.

steps.name: Measles through Central America
steps.page:
A measles epidemic swept New Spain and Central America in the early 1530s, striking populations already thinned by smallpox and by the labour demands of conquest.

Compound outbreaks of this kind — one disease arriving before a society had recovered from the last — are what made the American mortality so much higher than any single European epidemic.

steps.name: The cocoliztli of 1545
steps.page:
The deadliest epidemic recorded in the Americas began in 1545 and lasted three years. Nahua sources call it *cocoliztli*, a haemorrhagic fever with high fatality that affected Indigenous people far more than Spaniards.

Estimates of the dead across New Spain run to several million, with some 800,000 in the Valley of Mexico alone. Its cause is still argued over; one line of research points to an enteric fever, another to a native rodent-borne virus made worse by drought and forced labour.

steps.name: The Brazilian coast
steps.page:
Smallpox and an unidentified epidemic ran through the Tupi peoples of the Brazilian coast and the Jesuit mission villages in the early 1560s, together with a famine caused when nobody was well enough to plant.

The collapse of coastal Indigenous labour is one reason Portuguese sugar planters turned to importing enslaved Africans on a large scale.

steps.name: The cocoliztli of 1576
steps.page:
A second great cocoliztli epidemic ran from 1576 to about 1580 and killed perhaps two million people. It is far better documented than the first: the physician Francisco Hernández performed autopsies and left a clinical description.

By its end the Indigenous population of central Mexico was a small fraction of what it had been in 1519, and the colonial economy was being rebuilt around that fact.

name: Suleiman the Magnificent
summary: Suleiman I ruled the Ottoman Empire from 1520 to 1566, the longest reign of any sultan and the height of Ottoman power. His armies took Belgrade, Rhodes and most of Hungary; his fleets dominated the eastern Mediterranean.
body:
Part of [Ottoman Empire](event:ottoman-empire). Suleiman took Belgrade in 1521 and Rhodes in 1522, destroyed the Hungarian army at Mohács in 1526, and besieged Vienna without success in 1529 — roughly the limit of what an army could reach from Istanbul within a campaigning season. In the east he took Baghdad from the Safavids in 1534. He made a working alliance with France against the Habsburgs, and his admiral Hayreddin Barbarossa held the sea.

Ottomans knew him as *Kanuni*, the Lawgiver, for the codification of secular law that stood beside the sharia and regulated taxation, land tenure, and criminal penalties for his many non-Muslim subjects as well as his Muslim ones. His architect Sinan built the mosques that still define the skyline of Istanbul, and court poetry, miniature painting and Iznik tilework reached their high point.

The reign also sharpened the dynasty's succession problem: Suleiman had his eldest son Mustafa executed on suspicion of conspiracy, and the political weight of his wife Hurrem Sultan was without precedent. He died on campaign in Hungary in 1566, and the news was kept from the army until his successor was secure. The empire lasted until 1922, but it never again expanded as it had under him.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suleiman_the_Magnificent).

name: Fall of Tenochtitlan
summary: The Aztec capital Tenochtitlan fell to Hernán Cortés and his Indigenous allies on 13 August 1521, after a siege of about ninety-three days. The city was largely destroyed, and Mexico City was built on the ruins.
body:
Part of [Spanish conquest of the Americas](event:spanish-conquest). Cortés had entered the city peacefully in November 1519 and seized the emperor Moctezuma II as a hostage. The Spanish were driven out with heavy losses in the fighting of the *Noche Triste* in June 1520; they withdrew to Tlaxcala, a state that had resisted Aztec domination for generations, and returned with tens of thousands of Tlaxcalan and other allied troops.

Tenochtitlan stood on an island in Lake Texcoco, reached by three causeways and supplied with fresh water by an aqueduct. Cortés had thirteen brigantines built inland, carried to the lake in pieces, and used them to take control of the water; the causeways were then fought over yard by yard, and the aqueduct was cut. A smallpox epidemic had already killed a large part of the population, including the emperor Cuitláhuac, before the siege began.

The last emperor, Cuauhtémoc, was captured on 13 August 1521. The temples were pulled down and their stone used for a cathedral and a Spanish capital on the same site; the lake was drained over the following centuries, which is why Mexico City now subsides.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_of_Tenochtitlan).

name: Transatlantic slave trade
summary: Between the sixteenth century and the 1860s, European and American ships carried about 12.5 million enslaved Africans across the Atlantic; some 10.7 million survived the crossing. It was the largest forced migration in history, and it supplied the labour for the plantation economies of Brazil, the Caribbean and North America.
body:
Captives were bought on the African coast, mostly from African rulers and merchants who obtained them through war, raiding and judicial enslavement inland, in exchange for textiles, metalware, firearms and alcohol. They were held in coastal forts and barracoons and then packed below decks for the Middle Passage, a voyage of six to twelve weeks in which roughly one in eight died of dysentery, smallpox and dehydration. Ships carried plantation produce back to Europe — the triangle the trade is usually drawn as, though many individual voyages did not complete it.

Brazil received about 45 per cent of all captives and the Caribbean about a third; mainland North America took under 4 per cent, and its enslaved population grew mainly by natural increase, which was not the case further south. The traffic grew with sugar and peaked in the eighteenth century, when Portuguese, British and French ships carried the great majority. Ports from Lisbon and Nantes to Bristol and Liverpool grew on it, along with the credit, insurance and shipping businesses that financed it.

Its consequences ran both ways across the ocean: depopulation, militarisation and political disruption in parts of West and West Central Africa; and in the Americas, societies organised around racial slavery and the categories invented to justify it. Britain and the United States prohibited the trade in 1807 and 1808 and the Royal Navy's West Africa Squadron tried to suppress it; an illegal traffic to Brazil and Cuba continued for decades, and the last known slave ship reached Cuba in 1867. Slavery itself outlasted the trade — abolished in the British empire in 1833, in the [United States](event:us-civil-war) in 1865, in Brazil in 1888.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_slave_trade).

steps.name: The first direct crossings
steps.page:
Portuguese ships had carried enslaved Africans to Europe and the Atlantic islands since the 1440s. The first documented voyage direct from Africa to the Americas sailed in 1526, and a licensed traffic to the Spanish Caribbean followed.

Volumes were small by later standards — a few thousand a year — and much of the labour in early Spanish America was still Indigenous, under the *encomienda*.

steps.name: Sugar and the Brazilian trade
steps.page:
Sugar planting in north-eastern Brazil turned the trade into a system. Sugar is capital-intensive and brutal to work, and Portuguese planters replaced dying Indigenous labour with captives shipped from Angola and the Bight of Benin.

Brazil became the largest single destination and remained so for three centuries, taking about 45 per cent of all captives carried across the Atlantic.

steps.name: The Caribbean plantation boom
steps.page:
English and French colonists in Barbados, the Leewards and Saint-Domingue adopted sugar from the Dutch after 1640 and remade their islands as plantation economies within a generation. Small farms were bought out and the population became overwhelmingly enslaved and African.

Chartered companies — the Dutch WIC, the Royal African Company from 1672 — organised the supply, and colonial slave codes written in these decades fixed the legal status of enslaved people as property.

steps.name: The eighteenth-century peak
steps.page:
More than half of all captives were carried in the eighteenth century, most of them by Portuguese, British and French ships. Liverpool overtook Bristol and London as Britain's leading slaving port, and Nantes led in France.

The traffic drew in whole coastal economies. African states such as Dahomey, Asante and Oyo grew powerful on the exchange of captives for firearms and textiles, while raiding and war reached ever further inland to supply it.

steps.name: Abolition of the trade
steps.page:
After twenty years of campaigning by Quakers, evangelicals and formerly enslaved writers such as Olaudah Equiano — and after the [Haitian Revolution](event:haitian-revolution) had shown what slave societies risked — Parliament abolished the British slave trade in March 1807.

Denmark had prohibited it from 1803; the United States barred further imports from 1 January 1808, the earliest date its constitution allowed. Slavery itself was untouched in all three.

steps.name: Suppression and the last voyages
steps.page:
The Royal Navy's West Africa Squadron patrolled for six decades, intercepted about 1,600 ships and freed some 150,000 people, most of them landed at Freetown. It was expensive, and it made the passage more lethal as captains packed ships to outrun cruisers.

An illegal traffic to Brazil and Cuba continued regardless: over three million people were carried between 1810 and 1860. Brazil suppressed its own trade in 1850, and the last known slave ship reached Cuba in 1867.

name: Mughal Empire
summary: The Mughal dynasty, founded by Babur in 1526, ruled most of the Indian subcontinent for two centuries and presided over one of the richest states in the world. It survived in name until the British deposed the last emperor in 1857.
body:
Babur, a Timurid prince driven out of Ferghana, defeated the Delhi Sultanate at Panipat in 1526 with field artillery and mobile cavalry. His grandson [Akbar](event:akbar-great) built the machinery that turned conquest into an empire: the *mansabdari* system, which ranked officers by numerical grade and paid them from assigned revenues; a land tax assessed on measured yields; and a court open to Hindus, Jains, Parsis and Jesuits.

Under Jahangir and Shah Jahan the empire was probably the wealthiest state on earth, with perhaps a quarter of world manufacturing output, most of it cotton textiles woven for export. Its architecture — Fatehpur Sikri, the Red Fort, the [Taj Mahal](event:taj-mahal) — and its painting, gardens and Persian court culture set a style copied across Asia.

[Aurangzeb](event:aurangzeb-reign) extended Mughal rule over almost the whole subcontinent by 1700 and exhausted it doing so. After his death in 1707 the provinces became effectively independent, Nader Shah sacked Delhi in 1739 and took the peacock throne, and the Marathas held the initiative in the centre. The [East India Company](event:english-east-india) collected Bengal's revenues from 1765 and held Delhi itself by 1803; the emperor became a pensioner, and the title was abolished after the rebellion of 1857.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mughal_Empire).

name: Ethiopian–Adal War
summary: The Christian empire of Ethiopia and the Muslim Sultanate of Adal fought from 1529 to 1543 for control of the Ethiopian highlands, with Ottoman and Portuguese forces joining on opposite sides. Both states were ruined by it.
body:
Imam Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi, known in Ethiopia as Ahmad Gragn, the left-handed, led Adali forces out of the eastern lowlands and defeated the emperor Lebna Dengel at Shimbra Kure in 1529. Over the following decade his armies overran most of the highlands, burning churches and monasteries and forcing conversions; the emperor died a fugitive in the north in 1540.

Both sides drew in outside powers. The Ottomans, established at Zeila and along the Red Sea, supplied Adal with matchlocks, cannon and Turkish and Arab troops — the decisive advantage in the early campaigns. Ethiopia's appeals to Portugal, which had exchanged embassies with the court for decades, brought some four hundred musketeers under Cristóvão da Gama ashore at Massawa in 1541. Da Gama was captured and executed the following year, but the survivors joined the young emperor Gelawdewos, and at Wayna Daga in February 1543 Ahmad was shot dead. His army broke up within days.

The war left both states exhausted and much of the highlands depopulated. Into that vacuum moved the Oromo, whose migrations reshaped the region over the following century. Ethiopia kept its monarchy and its Orthodox church; Adal declined and fragmented; Ottoman authority never reached beyond the coastal strip.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopian%E2%80%93Adal_War).

name: Conquest of the Inca Empire
summary: Francisco Pizarro's force of fewer than two hundred men captured the Inca emperor Atahualpa at Cajamarca in November 1532, extracted an enormous ransom in gold and silver, and executed him. Cusco fell the following year.
body:
Part of [Spanish conquest of the Americas](event:spanish-conquest). The Inca empire was the largest state in the Americas, running four thousand kilometres along the Andes, but it had just emerged from a civil war between Atahualpa and his brother Huáscar. Smallpox spreading south ahead of the Europeans had already killed the emperor Huayna Capac and his designated heir, which is what began the succession war.

Atahualpa met the Spanish at Cajamarca on 16 November 1532 with a large but largely unarmed retinue, expecting to overawe them. Pizarro attacked from concealment with cavalry, cannon and steel, killed thousands in the enclosed square and took the emperor prisoner. Atahualpa offered to fill a room once with gold and twice with silver, and did so; the objects were melted into bullion. He was garrotted in July 1533 nonetheless, on charges of treason and idolatry.

The Spanish entered Cusco in November 1533 and ruled at first through puppet emperors drawn from the royal family. Manco Inca rebelled in 1536 and besieged the city for months before withdrawing into the forested mountains at Vilcabamba, where a rump Inca state survived until 1572.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_conquest_of_the_Inca_Empire).

name: Henry VIII breaks with Rome
summary: In 1534 the English Parliament declared Henry VIII Supreme Head of the Church of England, ending papal jurisdiction in the kingdom. The break began as a dispute over the king's marriage and ended by transferring the wealth of the monasteries to the crown.
body:
Part of [Protestant Reformation](event:reformation). Henry wanted his marriage to Catherine of Aragon annulled so that he could marry Anne Boleyn and get a male heir. Pope Clement VII, effectively in the power of Catherine's nephew the emperor Charles V, would not grant it. Thomas Cromwell's solution was statutory: acts passed between 1533 and 1534 cut off appeals to Rome, diverted church revenues to the crown, and made the king supreme head of the church in England.

The dissolution of the monasteries between 1536 and 1541 closed some 800 religious houses, seized their land and plate, and sold most of it to pay for war. It enriched the crown briefly and the gentry permanently, creating a landowning class with a material stake in the settlement, and it ended the monastic provision of charity, hospitality and schooling. Resistance was punished: Thomas More and John Fisher were executed for refusing the oath, and the northern rising called the Pilgrimage of Grace was put down after promises that were not kept.

Henry's own beliefs stayed broadly Catholic, and the Six Articles of 1539 reasserted traditional doctrine on pain of death. Protestant content came under his son Edward VI, was reversed under Mary I, and was settled in a deliberately ambiguous form under Elizabeth I from 1559.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Break_with_Rome).

name: The Scientific Revolution
summary: Between the middle of the sixteenth century and the end of the seventeenth, European natural philosophy replaced inherited authority with mathematics, observation and controlled experiment. Copernicus's heliocentric astronomy of 1543 is the conventional beginning and Newton's *Principia* of 1687 the conventional end.
body:
What changed was less the stock of facts than the standard of proof. Aristotle had been the authority on motion and Galen on the body; by 1700 an argument was expected to answer to measurement, and to measurements that other people could repeat. Instruments mattered as much as ideas: the telescope, the microscope, the air pump, the pendulum clock and the barometer each showed something no unaided sense could reach.

The mathematics was the deeper part. [Kepler](event:kepler) found that planets move on ellipses, [Galileo](event:galileo) that falling bodies accelerate uniformly and that motion persists without a cause, and [Newton](event:newton) that a single inverse-square law accounts for both. Descartes supplied coordinate geometry and a picture of the world as matter in motion; Bacon supplied a programme of organised, cooperative, published inquiry. Anatomy and chemistry followed the same route from authority to demonstration.

Institutions followed the ideas: the Accademia del Cimento in Florence, the Royal Society in London from 1660, the Académie des Sciences in Paris from 1666, and with them the scientific journal — the *Philosophical Transactions* began in 1665. Publication, criticism and replication became the ordinary practice of the subject and remain so. The confidence the new physics gave to reasoning about nature ran directly into the [Enlightenment](event:enlightenment).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scientific_Revolution).

steps.name: Copernicus places the Sun at the centre
Vesalius maps the human body
steps.page:
In the same year as Copernicus's book, Andreas Vesalius published *De humani corporis fabrica* at Basel — a description of human anatomy based on his own dissections, with plates by artists from Titian's workshop.

It corrected Galen in hundreds of particulars, most of them cases where Galen had dissected animals and assumed people were the same. The lesson was the method: look for yourself, and publish what you find rather than what the authority says.

steps.name: Tycho Brahe's observatory
steps.page:
Tycho Brahe built Uraniborg on the island of Hven with Danish royal funding and observed for twenty years with large graduated instruments and no telescope, reaching an accuracy of about one minute of arc.

His new star of 1572 and comet of 1577 showed that the heavens change and that comets pass through the crystalline spheres they were supposed to be bounded by. The observations themselves were the legacy: [Kepler](event:kepler) inherited them.

steps.name: Galileo turns a telescope on the sky
Bacon and Descartes on method
steps.page:
Francis Bacon's *Novum Organum* (1620) argued that knowledge of nature must be built up from organised observation and experiment, by many hands, and set against the biases he called idols of the mind.

René Descartes's *Discourse on Method* (1637) went the other way, from systematic doubt to certainty and thence to a world of matter in motion governed by geometry; its appendix introduced coordinate geometry. Between them they gave the century its two arguments about how to know anything.

steps.name: The Royal Society and the new institutions
steps.page:
The Royal Society was founded in London in 1660 to witness and record experiments collectively, taking as its motto *nullius in verba* — on no one's word. The Académie des Sciences followed in Paris in 1666.

Its *Philosophical Transactions*, begun in 1665, is the oldest scientific journal still published, and it established the practices the sciences still run on: dated priority, published method, and criticism by people who were not there.

name: Copernicus places the Sun at the centre
summary: Nicolaus Copernicus's *De revolutionibus orbium coelestium*, published in 1543 as he lay dying, argued that the Earth turns on its axis and orbits the Sun. It displaced the Earth from the centre of the universe and set the agenda for the astronomy of the next century.
body:
Part of [The Scientific Revolution](event:scientific-revolution). Copernicus was a canon at Frombork in Poland, trained in law and medicine, who worked at astronomy for decades without publishing. He had circulated a manuscript summary, the *Commentariolus*, around 1514; the full book appeared only at the urging of the young mathematician Rheticus, and it carried an unsigned preface by Andreas Osiander presenting the system as a calculating device rather than a claim about the world.

The model puts the Sun at the centre with the planets, Earth among them, in the order still taught, and explains naturally what Ptolemaic astronomy handled with added machinery: why Mercury and Venus never stray far from the Sun, and why the outer planets appear to reverse direction. It was not simpler to use. Copernicus kept perfectly circular orbits and so needed epicycles of his own, and his tables predicted no better than the ones they replaced.

The objections were serious rather than merely obstinate: a moving Earth should produce a visible shift in the fixed stars, and none could be measured until 1838. Acceptance took a century and the work of [Kepler](event:kepler), [Galileo](event:galileo) and [Newton](event:newton). The book was placed on the Index of Prohibited Books in 1616, pending correction.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicolaus_Copernicus).

name: Silver boom at Potosí
summary: Silver was found at Cerro Rico above Potosí, in what is now Bolivia, in 1545. For two centuries the mountain was the largest source of silver in the world, funding the Spanish crown and feeding a bullion flow that reached as far as China.
body:
The ore was rich and the site was terrible: a cone at 4,000 metres with no fuel, little water and a brutal climate. Potosí nevertheless became one of the largest cities in the world by 1600, with a population comparable to London's. From 1572 the viceroy Toledo introduced refining by mercury amalgamation, using mercury from Huancavelica, and reorganised labour under the *mita* — a rotating draft obliging Indigenous communities across a huge catchment to send a share of their adult men to the mines each year.

Mortality in the shafts and the refining yards was very high, from cave-ins, cold, silicosis and mercury poisoning, and whole communities were depopulated as families fled the draft or moved permanently to Potosí to avoid it. Enslaved Africans were also brought in, mainly to the mint. Estimates of the total number who died vary widely and are not securely established.

Between 1545 and 1810 Cerro Rico produced a large share of the world's silver, perhaps two-fifths. The metal paid Habsburg armies, passed through Seville to Genoese and Dutch bankers, and crossed the Pacific in the [Manila galleons](event:manila-galleon) to buy Chinese silk and porcelain, since China's tax system demanded payment in silver. It also helped drive a long European inflation. *Vale un Potosí* entered Spanish as the phrase for immense wealth.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD).

name: Council of Trent
summary: The Council of Trent met in three periods between 1545 and 1563 to answer the Reformation. It defined Catholic doctrine against Protestant positions and reformed the discipline and training of the clergy, setting the shape of the Roman church until the twentieth century.
body:
Part of [Protestant Reformation](event:reformation). On doctrine the council conceded nothing. It held that scripture and tradition are both sources of revelation, upheld the Latin Vulgate, defined the seven sacraments and transubstantiation, and rejected justification by faith alone — the point on which any reunion with Lutherans was least possible. It affirmed purgatory, the veneration of saints and the value of indulgences while forbidding their sale.

On practice it was severe with the church's own abuses. Bishops were required to live in their dioceses and forbidden to hold several sees at once; every diocese was to found a seminary to train priests, which is the origin of the modern clerical education; preaching was made a duty; and clandestine marriage was ended by requiring a parish priest and witnesses.

The council was slow and much interrupted — it sat in three periods, was suspended twice, and moved briefly to Bologna over an outbreak of plague — and it was overwhelmingly an Italian and Spanish assembly, with Protestants invited but never present on terms they would accept. Its decrees were promulgated in 1564 and produced a standard catechism, breviary and missal; the Latin Mass it fixed was used with little change until the Second Vatican Council in the 1960s.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Council_of_Trent).

name: Peace of Augsburg
summary: The Peace of Augsburg, agreed in September 1555, let each ruler in the Holy Roman Empire choose whether his territory would be Catholic or Lutheran. It ended a generation of religious war in Germany, at the cost of religious freedom for individuals.
body:
Part of [Protestant Reformation](event:reformation). The settlement followed the failure of Charles V's attempt to impose a religious solution by force: he had beaten the Protestant princes in 1547 and then lost the position when they allied with France. The peace is remembered by a later formula, *cuius regio, eius religio* — whose realm, his religion. Subjects who did not share their ruler's confession were granted the right to sell up and emigrate, which was the whole of the toleration on offer.

Two things were left out, and both mattered afterwards. Calvinism was not recognised at all, though it spread widely in the empire in the following decades. And the *ecclesiastical reservation* required any Catholic prince-bishop who converted to give up his lands — a clause the Protestant princes never accepted and both sides disputed for sixty years.

Charles V abdicated the following year, exhausted, dividing his inheritance between his brother Ferdinand in the empire and his son Philip II in Spain. The peace held in Germany for six decades, longer than anyone expected, until the disputes it had shelved broke open again in the [Thirty Years' War](event:thirty-years-war).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peace_of_Augsburg).

name: Akbar the Great reigns
summary: Akbar ruled the Mughal Empire from 1556 to 1605, extended it over most of northern and central India, and built the administration that held it together. His accommodation of non-Muslim subjects was unusual among rulers of his time.
body:
Part of [Mughal Empire](event:mughal-empire). Akbar came to the throne at thirteen and secured it at the second battle of Panipat in 1556. His campaigns took in Malwa, Gujarat, Bengal, Kashmir, most of Rajasthan and part of the Deccan. Rajput princes were brought in as allies and commanders rather than merely defeated, several through marriage — including the mother of his heir, who remained Hindu at court.

The machinery mattered more than the campaigns. The *mansabdari* system ranked officers by numerical grade, paid them from assigned revenue rather than from land they owned, and moved them about, keeping the nobility dependent on the throne. Todar Mal's revenue settlement taxed measured land on average yields, so that peasants knew their liability in advance. Akbar abolished the *jizya* poll tax on non-Muslims in 1564 and the tax on Hindu pilgrimage.

He was illiterate and had books read aloud to him, while assembling one of the great libraries of the age. His court at Fatehpur Sikri held debates between Muslims, Hindus, Jains, Zoroastrians and Jesuits, out of which he framed the *Din-i Ilahi*, a personal cult that attracted almost no followers. Orthodox clerics resented all of it. The empire he left his son was the wealthiest state in the world.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akbar).

name: William Shakespeare
summary: English playwright, poet and actor whose thirty-odd plays are the most performed and most translated body of work in any language.
body:
Shakespeare was born at Stratford-upon-Avon, the son of a glover, and married Anne Hathaway at eighteen. By the early 1590s he was in London as an actor and writer, and he became a shareholder in the Lord Chamberlain's Men — later the King's Men — which built the Globe on the south bank of the Thames.

[The plays](item:shakespeare) run from farce to the late romances by way of the English histories and the four great tragedies. Their reputation rests less on their plots, most of them borrowed, than on the invention of characters who appear to think in front of the audience, and on a use of English so productive that a few hundred words entered the language with them.

He wrote for a commercial theatre and seems not to have troubled about publication; half the plays survive only because two colleagues collected them in the First Folio of 1623, seven years after his death. He retired to Stratford as a prosperous man and is buried in the parish church there.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Shakespeare).

name: Manila Galleon trade route
summary: From 1565 to 1815 Spanish galleons sailed once or twice a year between Manila and Acapulco, carrying Chinese silk and porcelain east and American silver west. It was the first regular trade route across the Pacific and the link that closed a circuit of world commerce.
body:
The route depended on a discovery: in 1565 Andrés de Urdaneta found the return passage, sailing north from the Philippines to pick up the westerlies at about 40°N and then down the California coast. That crossing took four to six months and was one of the longest regular voyages under sail. Scurvy killed many crews, and the loss of a single galleon could ruin a year's commerce for both colonies.

Cargo was overwhelmingly Chinese, brought to Manila by junks from Fujian: silk above all, plus porcelain, lacquer, cotton and spices. It was paid for in [Potosí](event:potosi-silver) and Mexican silver, which China absorbed in enormous quantities because its taxes had to be paid in the metal. Goods were carried across Mexico to Veracruz and shipped on to Spain, so that the galleons joined the Pacific to the Atlantic and Asian manufactures to European buyers.

Spanish manufacturers complained that the traffic drained bullion to Asia, and the crown restricted the number and tonnage of ships without ever stopping it. Mexican silver dollars became a currency across East Asia. The last galleon sailed in 1815, during the wars of Spanish American independence.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manila_galleon).

name: Dutch Revolt against Spain
summary: The provinces of the Low Countries rebelled against Philip II of Spain in 1568. Eighty years of war followed. The seven northern provinces became an independent republic, recognised by Spain at the Peace of Münster in 1648, while the south remained Spanish.
body:
The revolt had religious, fiscal and constitutional causes at once. Calvinism had spread in the towns and been met with heresy laws; Philip's new taxes were resented; and the provinces' chartered privileges were being overridden by a distant king and his governors. The Duke of Alba's special tribunal — the Council of Troubles, known as the Council of Blood — executed over a thousand people and made compromise impossible.

The fighting was mostly about towns. Sieges rather than battles decided it, and the Dutch flooded their own land to stop armies; Spanish troops, unpaid when the silver fleets were late, mutinied repeatedly, and their sack of Antwerp in 1576 briefly drove all the provinces together. The Duke of Parma recovered the south for Spain in the 1580s but could not force the great rivers, and that line became the border between the modern Netherlands and Belgium.

What emerged in the north was a federation of provinces governed by their merchant regents, with the House of Orange holding military command — a republic in an age of kings. It financed the war with a public debt that lenders trusted at low interest, and its trade grew during it: the [East India Company](event:dutch-east-india) was chartered in 1602, in the middle of a war for survival. By 1648 it was the leading commercial power in Europe.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eighty_Years%27_War).

steps.name: Alba's tribunal and the first campaigns
steps.page:
The Duke of Alba's Council of Troubles condemned thousands and executed over a thousand, including the counts of Egmont and Hoorn, and his new tenth-penny sales tax united merchants against him.

William of Orange's invasions from Germany in 1568 failed, and the war seemed over before it had begun.

steps.name: The Sea Beggars take Brielle
steps.page:
Expelled from English ports, a fleet of exiled privateers called the Sea Beggars seized the little port of Brielle on 1 April 1572 almost by accident, finding it ungarrisoned.

Town after town in Holland and Zeeland then declared for Orange. The revolt had territory, and a coastline it could hold against an army that had no fleet.

steps.name: The Pacification of Ghent
steps.page:
Unpaid Spanish troops mutinied and sacked Antwerp in November 1576, killing several thousand people in what became known as the Spanish Fury.

Within days almost all seventeen provinces, Catholic and Protestant, signed the Pacification of Ghent demanding the withdrawal of foreign troops. It was the nearest the Low Countries came to holding together.

steps.name: Union of Utrecht and the Act of Abjuration
steps.page:
The unity did not last. Catholic southern provinces formed the Union of Arras in January 1579 and made terms with Spain; northern provinces answered days later with the Union of Utrecht, a defensive league that became the constitution of the Dutch Republic.

In July 1581 the States General passed the Act of Abjuration, declaring that a prince who oppresses his subjects forfeits their obedience, and renouncing Philip II.

steps.name: Parma's reconquest and the fall of Antwerp
steps.page:
The Duke of Parma, the ablest commander of the war, retook the southern cities one by one and closed on Antwerp, then the greatest port in northern Europe. It fell in August 1585 after a fourteen-month siege and a bridge of boats across the Scheldt.

Its Protestant merchants were given four years to leave, and most went north to Amsterdam with their capital and trade connections. The Dutch closed the Scheldt, and Antwerp's commerce never returned. Parma could not force the great rivers, and the line held there.

steps.name: The Twelve Years' Truce
steps.page:
Exhausted and bankrupt, Spain agreed a truce in April 1609 that treated the Republic as a state in all but name. The Dutch used the twelve years to expand their trade in Asia and the Atlantic.

At home the truce let a bitter religious and political quarrel between Remonstrants and Counter-Remonstrants come into the open, ending with the execution of the land's advocate, Oldenbarnevelt, in 1619.

steps.name: The Peace of Münster
steps.page:
War resumed in 1621 and merged into the [Thirty Years' War](event:thirty-years-war). Dutch fleets destroyed a Spanish armada in the Downs in 1639 and took Brazilian and Asian territory from the Portuguese.

By the treaty signed at Münster on 15 May 1648, Spain recognised the United Provinces as free and independent, ceded conquests in the south, and accepted the closure of the Scheldt. The Republic entered its golden age.

name: Battle of Lepanto
summary: On 7 October 1571 the fleet of a Catholic Holy League destroyed an Ottoman fleet in the Gulf of Patras off western Greece. It was the largest naval battle of the century and one of the last fought mainly by oared galleys.
body:
Part of [Ottoman Empire](event:ottoman-empire). The league was assembled by Pope Pius V after the Ottoman invasion of Venetian Cyprus, and drew ships from Spain, Venice, Genoa, the Papal States, Savoy and the Knights of Malta. Don John of Austria, half-brother of Philip II, commanded some 210 galleys against about 250 under Ali Pasha.

The Venetians brought six *galleasses* — large converted merchantmen carrying heavy guns on every side — and stationed them ahead of the line; their fire broke the Ottoman formation before the fleets met. After that the fighting was hand to hand across lashed decks. Ali Pasha was killed, most of the Ottoman fleet was captured or sunk, and some 12,000 Christian galley slaves were freed. Miguel de Cervantes, then a soldier, was shot twice in the chest and lost the use of his left hand.

Cyprus was not recovered, and the Ottomans had a new fleet at sea by the next campaigning season — a grand vizier is said to have remarked that Venice had merely singed his beard. What the battle ended was the belief in Christian Europe that the Ottoman navy could not be beaten. It was also the last great engagement of the galley age.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Lepanto).

name: Defeat of the Spanish Armada
summary: Philip II sent a fleet of about 130 ships in 1588 to escort an invasion army from the Netherlands to England. English gunnery, fireships and Atlantic weather broke it up, and roughly half the ships never returned to Spain.
body:
Part of [Protestant Reformation](event:reformation). The expedition answered English raiding of Spanish shipping and treasure, English support for the [Dutch revolt](event:netherlands-independence), and the execution of Mary, Queen of Scots, in 1587. The plan required the fleet to reach the Flemish coast and ferry the Duke of Parma's veteran army across the Channel — but Parma's barges could not get out past Dutch shallow-draught blockaders, and there was no deep-water port the Armada could hold while it waited.

The Spanish came up the Channel in July in a crescent formation that the English could not break, fighting running actions at long range with little effect on either side. The Armada anchored off Calais; at midnight eight English fireships were sent in, and the Spanish cut their cables and scattered. The battle of Gravelines the next day did real damage at close range. With the wind against them and their anchors gone, the survivors ran north around Scotland and Ireland, where storms wrecked many ships on the coast.

England's danger was not over — further armadas sailed in the 1590s, and Spain remained the greater power for another half-century — but the defeat became a founding story of English Protestant identity. The commemorative medal read: *He blew with His winds, and they were scattered*.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_Armada).

name: Shakespeare's plays
summary: William Shakespeare wrote about thirty-eight plays for the London commercial theatre between roughly 1589 and 1613. They are the most performed and most translated body of drama in any language.
body:
[Shakespeare](item:william-shakespeare) wrote for a repertory company he part-owned — the Lord Chamberlain's Men, renamed the King's Men on James I's accession in 1603 — which played at the Theatre, then at the Globe from 1599, and at the indoor Blackfriars from 1608. This was commercial work for a mixed audience standing in the yard and seated in the galleries, performed in daylight on a bare stage with almost no scenery, where place is established by the words.

The usual grouping is comedies, histories and tragedies, with the late plays — *The Winter's Tale*, *The Tempest* — set apart as romances. Almost every plot is borrowed, from Holinshed's chronicles, from Plutarch, from Italian novellas. What is not borrowed is the language and the interiority: soliloquy is used to show a mind changing while it speaks, in *Hamlet* and *Macbeth* above all.

About half the plays were unpublished when he died in 1616, and survive only because two fellow actors, John Heminges and Henry Condell, collected thirty-six of them in the First Folio of 1623. Adapted, cut, rewritten with happy endings and restored again over four centuries, they have never left the stage.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shakespeare%27s_plays).

name: Edict of Nantes
summary: Henry IV of France issued the Edict of Nantes in April 1598, granting Huguenots freedom of conscience, limited freedom of worship and equal civil rights. It ended the French Wars of Religion, which had run for thirty-six years.
body:
Part of [Protestant Reformation](event:reformation). Henry was himself a Huguenot who had converted to Catholicism in 1593 to secure Paris and the throne. The edict allowed Protestant worship where it was already established and in one town per judicial district, but not in Paris; it opened offices and universities to Huguenots and gave them courts of mixed membership to hear their cases. Secret articles granted them some 150 fortified towns, garrisoned at royal expense — a state within the state, and the part Catholics found intolerable.

The military privileges were removed by Louis XIII after the siege of La Rochelle in 1628, though the religious clauses stood. Louis XIV then dismantled those too, first by harassment and forced billeting, and in 1685 revoked the edict outright by the Edict of Fontainebleau, ordering churches pulled down, ministers exiled and Protestant children baptised as Catholics.

Perhaps 200,000 Huguenots left France for England, the Dutch Republic, Prussia, Switzerland and the American colonies, taking skills in weaving, watchmaking, printing and finance with them. The edict was one of the earliest laws in Europe to give a religious minority a legal standing, and its revocation was read across Protestant Europe as a demonstration of what royal absolutism was worth.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edict_of_Nantes).

name: English East India Company founded
summary: Elizabeth I chartered the East India Company in December 1600 as a joint-stock venture for trade with Asia. Over two centuries it became a territorial power, ruling much of India with its own armies, until the Crown took over in 1858.
body:
The company began with a monopoly of English trade east of the Cape of Good Hope and a handful of ships. Pushed out of the spice islands by the Dutch — the killing of English merchants at Amboyna in 1623 settled that contest — it concentrated on India, trading silver and bullion for cotton textiles, indigo, saltpetre and later tea, from factories at Surat, Madras, Bombay and Calcutta held by permission of Indian rulers and defended by small garrisons.

Its transformation came in Bengal. Victory at [Plassey](event:battle-plassey) in 1757 made the company the power behind the nawab, and in 1765 it obtained the *diwani* — the right to collect the revenues of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa. From then it taxed and governed as well as traded, and paid for its Indian armies out of Indian revenue. The Bengal famine of 1770, in which perhaps a third of the province died, followed within five years.

Parliament regulated it in stages — the Regulating Act of 1773, Pitt's India Act of 1784, the impeachment of Warren Hastings — and stripped its trade monopolies in 1813 and 1833, leaving it an administration with a private army of over 200,000 men. After the rebellion of 1857 it was wound up and India passed directly to the Crown.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company).

name: Dutch East India Company founded
summary: The Dutch East India Company (VOC) was chartered in 1602 with a monopoly of Dutch trade in Asia and the power to make war, sign treaties and plant colonies on its own account. It is usually described as the first company with permanent, publicly traded shares.
body:
The charter merged competing Dutch ventures into one and granted twenty-one years of monopoly, renewed repeatedly thereafter. Its shares traded on the Amsterdam exchange, which developed forward contracts, short selling and the rest of the machinery of a securities market around them. Capital was permanent rather than repaid after each voyage, which is what allowed the company to build forts, fleets and a standing administration.

It pursued monopoly by force. Jan Pieterszoon Coen founded Batavia on the ruins of Jayakarta in 1619, and in 1621 destroyed the population of the Banda Islands — killed, starved or deported — to take the nutmeg trade, repopulating the islands with enslaved labour under Dutch planters. The company took Malacca from Portugal in 1641, held the Cape from 1652, and from 1641 had the only European access to Japan, at Dejima in Nagasaki harbour.

At its height it employed tens of thousands, sent about a million Europeans east, and paid steady dividends for most of two centuries. War with Britain, corruption among its servants and the cost of governing territory in Java eroded it, and it was dissolved in 1799, its debts and possessions passing to the Dutch state.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_East_India_Company).

name: Tokugawa Japan and sakoku
summary: The Tokugawa shoguns ruled Japan from Edo, now Tokyo, from 1603 to 1868. They kept internal peace for two and a half centuries and, from the 1630s, restricted foreign contact almost to nothing — the policy later called *sakoku*, the closed country.
body:
Tokugawa Ieyasu won at Sekigahara in 1600 and took the title of shogun in 1603. The regime controlled some 260 daimyo domains through hostage-taking and expense: *sankin-kotai* required each lord to spend alternate years at Edo and to leave his family there permanently, and the processions and double households consumed the wealth that might have paid for rebellion. Society was ordered in fixed status groups; the emperor remained at Kyoto without power.

Christianity was suppressed after the Shimabara rebellion of 1637–38, Japanese were forbidden to leave or return, and foreign trade was confined to a Dutch post on the artificial island of Dejima together with Chinese, Korean and Ryukyuan channels. The country was not sealed so much as tightly licensed. Peace brought a long expansion of cities, roads, commerce and literacy, of kabuki and woodblock printing, and of *rangaku* — Dutch learning — through which European anatomy and astronomy reached Japanese scholars.

By the nineteenth century the samurai were indebted, the currency was debased and famine had provoked risings. Commodore Perry's American squadron forced the ports open in 1853–54, unequal treaties followed, and the discredited shogunate fell to domains from the south-west in the [Meiji Restoration](event:meiji) of 1868.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edo_period).

name: Jamestown settlement
summary: Jamestown, founded in May 1607 on a river in Virginia, was the first permanent English settlement in North America. It nearly failed several times before tobacco made it viable, and it became the capital of the colony of Virginia.
body:
Part of [Age of Discovery](event:age-of-discovery). The Virginia Company sent about a hundred men and boys to look for gold and a passage to the Pacific. The site they chose was defensible and malarial, with brackish water. Most of the first arrivals were dead within a year of disease, hunger and fighting, and in the starving time of the winter of 1609–10 the population fell from several hundred to about sixty; the survivors were boarding ship to abandon the place when a relief fleet arrived.

John Rolfe's planting of a West Indian tobacco variety from 1612 gave Virginia an export. Tobacco is labour-intensive and exhausts soil, so the colony spread along the rivers and needed workers: indentured servants at first, and from 1619, when an English privateer sold some twenty captive Africans at Point Comfort, enslaved Africans in slowly growing numbers. The first representative assembly in English America met at Jamestown the same year.

The Powhatan confederacy, the region's dominant power, attacked in 1622 and again in 1644, killing hundreds of colonists; both were answered with wars of destruction that broke Powhatan power. The capital moved to Williamsburg in 1699 after the statehouse burned, and Jamestown was abandoned to farmland.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamestown,_Virginia).

name: Founding of Quebec
summary: Samuel de Champlain founded Quebec on the St Lawrence in July 1608 as a fur-trading post. It became the capital of New France and the centre of French settlement in North America.
body:
Part of [Age of Discovery](event:age-of-discovery). Champlain chose a narrowing of the river below a cliff — *kébec* in Algonquian means where the water narrows — which could be defended and could control traffic upstream. Twenty of the first twenty-eight men died of scurvy in the first winter.

The colony lived on beaver pelts, and pelts depended on Indigenous hunters and middlemen, so the French built alliances rather than plantations: with the Innu, the Algonquin and above all the Huron-Wendat. Champlain joined a war party against the Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) in 1609, which set the alignment of the next century's conflicts. *Coureurs de bois* travelled and traded deep into the interior, Jesuit missionaries followed them, and the resulting intermarriage produced the Métis peoples of the west.

New France grew slowly — around 70,000 settlers by the 1750s, against well over a million in the British colonies — because the fur trade needed few people and the church discouraged Protestant emigration. Britain took Quebec in 1759 at the battle of the Plains of Abraham during the [Seven Years' War](event:seven-years-war) and kept it in 1763, but the Quebec Act of 1774 preserved French civil law, the language and the Catholic church, and Quebec remains the heart of Francophone North America.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quebec_City#Colonial_era).

name: Kepler's laws of planetary motion
summary: Johannes Kepler published three laws describing how planets move: on ellipses with the Sun at one focus, sweeping equal areas in equal times, with orbital period fixed by distance from the Sun. They replaced two thousand years of circles.
body:
Part of [The Scientific Revolution](event:scientific-revolution). Kepler worked from the observations of Tycho Brahe, the most accurate made before the telescope, which he inherited when Tycho died in 1601. Fitting Mars to a circular orbit left a residual error of eight minutes of arc — a discrepancy earlier astronomers would have set aside, and which Kepler took as decisive. The ellipse and the equal-area law appeared in *Astronomia nova* in 1609; the third law, that the square of a planet's period is proportional to the cube of its mean distance, in *Harmonices mundi* in 1619.

He worked on much else. He explained how the eye forms an image on the retina, designed an improved telescope with two convex lenses, wrote on the packing of spheres and on snowflakes, and calculated the *Rudolphine Tables*, far more accurate than anything before them. He believed to the end in a cosmos built on geometric and musical harmony, and he spent a year defending his mother at her trial for witchcraft.

The laws were empirical: they described how the planets move without saying why. [Newton](event:newton) derived all three from the inverse-square law of gravitation in 1687, which is how Kepler's work became part of physics.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kepler%27s_laws_of_planetary_motion).
