name: Galileo turns a telescope on the sky
summary: In 1610 Galileo Galilei turned a telescope of his own making on the sky and published what he saw: mountains on the Moon, four moons circling Jupiter, and stars beyond counting in the Milky Way. The phases of Venus followed. The heavens were neither perfect nor centred on the Earth.
body:
Part of [The Scientific Revolution](event:scientific-revolution). Galileo did not invent the telescope but ground better lenses and reached about twenty times magnification. *Sidereus Nuncius*, published in March 1610, made him famous across Europe within months. The moons of Jupiter mattered most: here was plainly a centre of motion that was not the Earth. The phases of Venus, observed later that year, cannot occur at all in the Ptolemaic arrangement.

He also did the physics. Bodies of different weight fall alike; a body in motion stays in motion unless something stops it; a projectile follows a parabola compounded of uniform and accelerated motion. Establishing that mathematics describes terrestrial motion was as large a contribution as the observations, and it is what [Newton](event:newton) built on.

His advocacy of [Copernicus](event:copernicus) brought a warning from the Inquisition in 1616. When his *Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems* appeared in 1632, with the pope's own argument given to a character named Simplicio, he was tried, made to abjure kneeling, and confined to his villa near Florence for the last nine years of his life. He was blind by 1638 and finished his best book on mechanics, the *Two New Sciences*, under house arrest; it was smuggled out and printed in the Netherlands.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galileo_Galilei).

name: Thirty Years' War
summary: The Thirty Years' War began in 1618 with a revolt in Bohemia and drew in most of Europe before ending at the Peace of Westphalia in 1648. It was fought largely inside the Holy Roman Empire, where armies living off the land brought famine and epidemic; parts of Germany lost a third or more of their people.
body:
Part of [Protestant Reformation](event:reformation). It began as a constitutional and religious quarrel within the empire: the Bohemian estates rejected the Catholic Habsburg Ferdinand as their king and elected the Calvinist Frederick of the Palatinate instead. It became a European war because the Habsburgs of Vienna and Madrid were allies, and because Denmark, Sweden and finally France each intervened rather than let the emperor consolidate power in Germany. France, though Catholic, subsidised the Protestant side for years before joining it openly in 1635.

The armies were large, mercenary and irregularly paid, and were supplied by *contribution* — money and food extracted from whatever territory they stood on, friendly or not. That, with the typhus, plague and dysentery that travelled with them, did most of the killing; the sack of Magdeburg in 1631, in which some 20,000 died, became the war's byword. Wallenstein raised armies as a business venture and was murdered on the emperor's orders when he grew too independent to control.

The settlement of 1648 confirmed the [Peace of Augsburg](event:peace-augsburg), added Calvinism to the recognised confessions, and left the imperial princes with effective sovereignty. Spain recognised Dutch independence; France gained in Alsace and Sweden on the Baltic coast. The empire continued as a legal framework rather than a state, and later writers made 1648 the founding date of a European order of sovereign powers.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thirty_Years%27_War).

steps.name: The Bohemian revolt
steps.page:
Protestant nobles threw two imperial governors and a secretary out of a window of Prague Castle on 23 May 1618 — the Defenestration of Prague; all three survived the fall. The estates then deposed the Habsburg Ferdinand and elected Frederick V of the Palatinate king of Bohemia.

Ferdinand, now also emperor, borrowed a Catholic League army under Tilly and Spanish help. Frederick's forces were destroyed at the White Mountain outside Prague on 8 November 1620, and twenty-seven leaders of the revolt were executed in the old town square.

steps.name: The Palatinate campaign
steps.page:
Spanish troops from the Netherlands and imperial armies overran Frederick's own lands on the Rhine while he was losing Bohemia, and Tilly beat his remaining supporters at Wimpfen and Höchst in 1622 and Stadtlohn in 1623.

Frederick's electoral title was transferred to Maximilian of Bavaria, upsetting the confessional balance of the electoral college and giving every Protestant prince a reason to fear the next imperial decision.

steps.name: Danish intervention
steps.page:
Christian IV of Denmark, who was also a duke of the empire and wanted the north German bishoprics for his family, entered the war in 1625 with English and Dutch subsidies.

He was beaten by Tilly at Lutter in 1626 while Wallenstein's new army overran Jutland, and made peace at Lübeck in 1629 on terms that cost him nothing but influence. Emboldened, Ferdinand issued the Edict of Restitution, ordering the return of all church land secularised since 1552 — the demand that made a compromise peace impossible.

steps.name: Gustavus Adolphus and the Swedish intervention
steps.page:
Gustavus Adolphus landed in Pomerania in July 1630, financed by France, with an army trained in mobile artillery and combined infantry and cavalry volleys. The sack of Magdeburg in May 1631 by imperial forces, in which some 20,000 died, drove the wavering Protestant electors into his camp.

He destroyed Tilly's army at Breitenfeld in September 1631 and swept to the Rhine and into Bavaria. He was killed leading a cavalry charge in fog at Lützen on 16 November 1632, in a battle his army won.

steps.name: Nördlingen and the Peace of Prague
steps.page:
A Spanish-imperial army crushed the Swedes and their German allies at Nördlingen in September 1634, ending Swedish dominance in the south.

The Peace of Prague in May 1635 suspended the Edict of Restitution, reconciled Saxony and most Lutheran princes with the emperor, and might have ended the war as a German conflict. France declared war on Spain within days.

steps.name: French intervention
steps.page:
Richelieu had subsidised the emperor's enemies for a decade; from 1635 France fought openly, allied with Sweden and the Dutch, and the war lost most of its religious character.

Thirteen more years of campaigning followed across Germany, the Rhineland, the Spanish Netherlands and northern Italy, fought by armies that lived off the countryside. Condé's victory at Rocroi in 1643 broke the reputation of the Spanish infantry, and negotiations opened in Westphalia the same year while the fighting went on.

name: Harvey discovers blood circulation
summary: William Harvey showed in 1628 that blood circulates: it is driven by the heart out through the arteries and returns through the veins, in a closed loop. The demonstration overturned the account of the body taught since Galen.
body:
Part of [The Scientific Revolution](event:scientific-revolution). Galen had held that blood is manufactured continuously in the liver from food, moves outward through the veins and is consumed by the tissues, and that some seeps through invisible pores in the wall between the ventricles. Harvey's decisive argument was quantitative: he measured the capacity of the heart, multiplied by the pulse rate, and found that it moves more than the body's own weight of blood in an hour. No liver could make that. The same blood must be coming back.

He supported it with dissection, with vivisection of cold-blooded animals whose hearts beat slowly enough to watch, and with a demonstration anyone could repeat: a ligature on the arm makes the veins stand out, and their valves can be shown to admit blood only towards the heart. *Exercitatio anatomica de motu cordis et sanguinis in animalibus* was printed at Frankfurt in 1628, when Harvey was fifty and physician to Charles I.

One link was missing: he could not see how blood crossed from arteries to veins and had to infer it. Marcello Malpighi found the capillaries with a microscope in 1661, four years after Harvey's death. The book is a founding text of experimental physiology.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Harvey).

name: Taj Mahal built
summary: The Taj Mahal is a marble mausoleum at Agra, built by the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan for his wife Mumtaz Mahal, who died in childbirth in 1631. Work began in 1632 and the complex was finished about 1653.
body:
Part of [Mughal Empire](event:mughal-empire). The tomb stands on a terrace above the Yamuna, faced in white marble quarried at Makrana and inlaid with jasper, jade, turquoise and lapis in floral patterns — *pietra dura*, worked by craftsmen from as far as Italy and Persia. The Quranic inscriptions in black marble are cut with letters enlarged as they rise, so that they appear even in height from the ground. The four minarets lean very slightly outward, which would carry them away from the tomb if they fell. A mosque and a matching guest hall in red sandstone flank it, and a *charbagh* garden divided by water channels lies in front.

The chief architect is usually given as Ustad Ahmad Lahauri. Contemporary accounts speak of some 20,000 workers and of materials brought by a thousand elephants. The whole is laid out symmetrically, an order broken only by Shah Jahan's own cenotaph, placed beside his wife's after his death.

Shah Jahan was deposed by his son [Aurangzeb](event:aurangzeb-reign) in 1658 and spent his last years confined in Agra Fort within sight of it. The building was neglected and looted in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, restored under Curzon around 1900, and is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site visited by millions a year.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taj_Mahal).

name: English Civil War
summary: Parliament and Charles I fought three civil wars in England, Scotland and Ireland between 1642 and 1651. Parliament won; the king was tried and beheaded in 1649, and the three kingdoms were governed as a republic until the monarchy was restored in 1660.
body:
The quarrel was over money, religion and the limits of royal power at once. Charles ruled for eleven years without calling Parliament, raising revenue by expedients such as ship money, and was forced to recall it in 1640 only when a war he had provoked with Scotland over prayer-book reform went badly. Parliament's demands escalated; a rebellion in Ireland in 1641 raised the question of who should command the army sent to suppress it; and the king raised his standard at Nottingham in August 1642.

Parliament's advantages were London, the navy, the customs and the wealth of the south-east. Its instrument was the New Model Army, formed in 1645: professional, regularly paid, promoted on merit and full of religious radicals, with Oliver Cromwell rising through its cavalry. The king was beaten at Marston Moor and Naseby, then made a deal with the Scots that produced a second war in 1648, after which the army purged Parliament, tried him for treason and executed him on 30 January 1649 — the first European monarch put to death by judicial sentence of his own subjects.

The Commonwealth that followed conquered Ireland and Scotland and settled into Cromwell's Protectorate. It did not outlive him: his son resigned, the army split, and Charles II was restored in 1660. The constitutional questions were reopened in 1688 and settled then.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Civil_War).

steps.name: The first war opens
steps.page:
Charles I raised his standard at Nottingham on 22 August 1642 after Parliament had claimed control of the militia. The country divided by region and by interest rather than cleanly: London, the ports and the cloth towns mostly for Parliament, the north and west mostly for the king.

The first pitched battle, at Edgehill on 23 October, was indecisive, and the king's advance on London was turned back at Turnham Green the following month.

steps.name: Marston Moor
steps.page:
Parliament bought Scottish intervention with the Solemn League and Covenant, promising a Presbyterian settlement. The combined armies met Prince Rupert outside York on 2 July 1644 in the largest battle ever fought on English soil.

Cromwell's cavalry broke the royalist right and then turned on the rest. The king lost the north of England in an evening, and Cromwell's reputation was made.

steps.name: The New Model Army and Naseby
steps.page:
Parliament reorganised its forces in February 1645 into a single national army, paid regularly from a national assessment, promoted on merit, and separated from Parliament by the Self-Denying Ordinance.

It destroyed the king's main field army at Naseby on 14 June. His private correspondence was captured with the baggage and published, showing that he had been seeking Irish and Continental troops. The first war ended with his surrender to the Scots in 1646.

steps.name: The second civil war
steps.page:
From captivity Charles negotiated with everyone at once and in December 1647 made an Engagement with the Scots, who invaded on his behalf. Royalist risings broke out in Kent, Essex and South Wales in the spring of 1648.

Cromwell scattered the Scottish army at Preston in August. The army now regarded the king as a man of blood who had renewed a war he had lost, and it would no longer treat with him.

steps.name: The trial and execution of Charles I
steps.page:
Colonel Pride excluded the members who still wanted a settlement with the king, and the remaining Rump established a High Court of Justice. Charles refused to plead, denying that any court could try its sovereign.

He was beheaded outside the Banqueting House in Whitehall on 30 January 1649, wearing two shirts against the cold so that he would not be seen to shiver. The monarchy and the House of Lords were abolished, and England was declared a commonwealth.

steps.name: The conquest of Ireland
steps.page:
Cromwell landed near Dublin in August 1649 to reconquer Ireland, where a Catholic confederacy had allied with royalists. The garrisons of Drogheda and Wexford were put to the sword, and the storming of Drogheda in particular was publicised as a warning to others.

The war and the famine and plague that came with it killed a very large share of the Irish population, and the settlement that followed transferred most Catholic-owned land to Protestant creditors and soldiers. It is remembered in Ireland as the bitterest episode of the century.

steps.name: Dunbar and Worcester
steps.page:
The Scots proclaimed Charles II king and took him on Presbyterian terms. Cromwell invaded, was cornered at Dunbar in September 1650 and destroyed a much larger Scottish army there in a dawn attack.

Charles marched south with a new army the following summer and was beaten at Worcester on 3 September 1651, exactly a year later. He escaped abroad after six weeks in hiding. The wars were over, and the three kingdoms were ruled from London until 1660.

name: Isaac Newton
summary: English mathematician and physicist who set out the laws of motion and universal gravitation, and who invented the calculus independently of Leibniz.
body:
Newton was born at Woolsthorpe in Lincolnshire on Christmas Day 1642 by the calendar then used in England, which is 4 January 1643 by the one used now. He went up to Trinity College, Cambridge, and did much of his most original work in 1665–67, when plague closed the university and he returned home.

The *[Principia](item:newton)* of 1687 gave three laws of motion and a law of universal gravitation, and showed that the same mathematics governs a falling apple, the tides, comets and the orbits of the planets. It is the central text of the [Scientific Revolution](item:scientific-revolution). To carry out the work he developed what he called fluxions — the [calculus](item:calculus), which Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz reached independently and published first, provoking a bitter priority dispute.

He also wrote the *Opticks*, demonstrated that white light is a mixture of colours, built the first reflecting telescope, spent decades on alchemy and biblical chronology, sat in Parliament, and ran the Royal Mint, where he pursued counterfeiters with some enthusiasm. He was President of the Royal Society from 1703 until his death.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isaac_Newton).

name: Qing dynasty
summary: The Qing were a Manchu dynasty that conquered Ming China from 1644 and ruled until 1912, the last of the imperial dynasties. Under them the empire reached its greatest size, taking in Mongolia, Xinjiang, Tibet and Taiwan, and its population grew from perhaps 150 million to over 400 million.
body:
The Manchus were a confederation from the north-east who entered Beijing in 1644 amid a peasant rebellion that had already destroyed the Ming; resistance in the south lasted four decades. They ruled as a conquest elite: Manchu and Han were kept legally distinct, banner garrisons held the cities, Han men were required to shave the forehead and wear the queue on pain of death, and Manchu shared official business with Chinese. But the Confucian examination bureaucracy was kept intact, which is why the state functioned.

The long reigns of [Kangxi](event:kangxi-emperor), [Yongzheng](event:yongzheng-reforms) and Qianlong covered most of the eighteenth century — a period of peace, territorial expansion and rapid population growth, helped by New World crops such as maize and sweet potato that grew on land rice could not use. Vast scholarly compilations were sponsored, and literary inquisitions ran alongside them.

Pressure came from several directions at once in the nineteenth century: rural poverty and land hunger, a silver drain and the [Opium Wars](event:opium-wars), which opened the treaty ports and exposed the gap in military technology, and then the [Taiping Rebellion](event:taiping), which may have killed twenty million people. Reform came late and partially. The dynasty was overthrown by the revolution of 1911, and the last emperor abdicated in February 1912.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qing_dynasty).

name: Peace of Westphalia
summary: The Peace of Westphalia was concluded in October 1648 by two treaties signed at Münster and Osnabrück. It ended the Thirty Years' War in the Holy Roman Empire and, in a separate treaty, the Eighty Years' War between Spain and the Dutch Republic.
body:
Part of [Thirty Years' War](event:thirty-years-war). The negotiations lasted about five years and are usually counted the first modern peace congress: delegations from most of Europe, meeting simultaneously in two Westphalian towns because Catholic and Protestant parties would not sit together, working through mediators and agreed protocols.

The terms were specific rather than philosophical. The [Peace of Augsburg](event:peace-augsburg) was restored and extended to Calvinists, and the religious position of 1624 was made the benchmark for who held what. Imperial princes gained the right to conduct their own foreign policy short of alliances against the emperor. France took Habsburg rights in Alsace and Sweden took territory on the Baltic coast, both with seats in the imperial diet. Spain recognised the independence of the Dutch Republic, and the separation of the Swiss cantons from the empire was confirmed.

Later writers made Westphalia the origin of a system of sovereign states that recognise no superior and do not interfere in one another's internal affairs — "Westphalian sovereignty". Historians have pointed out that the treaties say nothing so general, and that the empire went on as a legal order above its princes for another century and a half. The label has stuck anyway, and it names something real about how European diplomacy worked afterwards.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peace_of_Westphalia).

name: Aurangzeb expands the Mughal Empire
summary: Aurangzeb ruled the Mughal Empire from 1658 to 1707 and extended it over almost the whole Indian subcontinent. The wars that did it drained the treasury, and his enforcement of Islamic orthodoxy alienated Hindu and Sikh subjects; the empire broke apart soon after his death.
body:
Part of [Mughal Empire](event:mughal-empire). He took the throne by defeating his brothers in a war of succession and imprisoning his father Shah Jahan in Agra Fort. He lived austerely by the standards of his dynasty, copied Qurans and sewed caps to earn his own keep, and cared little for the painting and music his predecessors had patronised.

He reversed much of [Akbar](event:akbar-great)'s accommodation. The *jizya* on non-Muslims was reimposed in 1679, a number of temples were destroyed, court music was curtailed, and the ninth Sikh guru, Tegh Bahadur, was executed in 1675 — which turned the Sikh community towards armed organisation. He faced a Rajput revolt, a long Sikh war, and the Marathas under Shivaji, whose mobile raiding he could never bring to a decision.

From 1681 he moved his court permanently to the Deccan and spent twenty-six years there, annexing Bijapur and Golconda but never ending Maratha resistance. The empire reached its greatest extent and its greatest strain together: the *mansabdari* system had more claimants than assignable revenue, and an army in the field for a generation ate the surplus that paid for it. Within decades of his death in 1707 the provinces were effectively independent, and the [East India Company](event:english-east-india) began dealing with them one at a time.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aurangzeb).

name: Kangxi Emperor consolidates Qing Dynasty
summary: The Kangxi Emperor reigned from 1661 to 1722, one of the longest reigns in Chinese history. He crushed the revolt that threatened Qing rule in the south, annexed Taiwan, checked Russian expansion and campaigned in Mongolia, leaving a consolidated and prosperous empire.
body:
Part of [Qing dynasty](event:qing-dynasty). He came to the throne at seven under regents and took power himself at fifteen. The Revolt of the Three Feudatories — a rising of the Han generals who had helped the Manchus conquer the south — took eight years to put down, from 1673 to 1681, and nearly undid the dynasty. Taiwan, the last Ming loyalist base, was taken in 1683. The Treaty of Nerchinsk with Russia in 1689, negotiated in Latin through Jesuit intermediaries, fixed the Amur frontier and was the first treaty China concluded with a European power on equal terms. Campaigns against the Dzungars carried Qing power deep into Mongolia.

He cut taxes repeatedly and in 1712 froze the head-tax quota permanently, repaired the Yellow River works, toured the south six times, and sponsored the Kangxi Dictionary and vast compilations of literature and cartography. He employed Jesuits as astronomers and mathematicians and studied Euclid with them, but ended toleration of Christian missions when Rome forbade Chinese converts to honour their ancestors.

His last years were spoiled by the struggle among his many sons over the succession, which he twice tried and failed to settle. [Yongzheng](event:yongzheng-reforms) succeeded him in 1722 in circumstances still argued over.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kangxi_Emperor).

name: Boyle's law of gases
summary: Robert Boyle published in 1662 the relation that the volume of a fixed quantity of gas varies inversely with its pressure at constant temperature. It was one of the first quantitative laws to come out of a designed experiment.
body:
Part of [The Scientific Revolution](event:scientific-revolution). Boyle worked at Oxford with an air pump built for him by Robert Hooke, and used it to show that air has weight and springiness, that sound will not travel in a vacuum, and that neither a flame nor a small animal survives without it. The pressure–volume relation came from a different apparatus: a J-shaped glass tube in which poured mercury compressed a trapped column of air, so that pressure and volume could both be read off and compared. The idea had been put to him by Richard Towneley and Henry Power, which Boyle acknowledged in print; on the Continent the same law is often credited to Edme Mariotte.

*The Sceptical Chymist* (1661) attacked the four Aristotelian elements and the alchemists' three principles alike, argued for treating matter as corpuscles, and insisted that chemical claims be settled by experiment. Boyle also insisted on describing apparatus and procedure in enough detail for others to repeat the work, including experiments that failed — a habit as consequential as any result.

A founder member of the Royal Society, he stands between alchemy and chemistry, since he pursued transmutation as well. His law later became one leg of the ideal gas law.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boyle%27s_law).

name: Robert Hooke discovers cells
summary: Robert Hooke's *Micrographia*, published in 1665, showed readers what a microscope could see. Examining a slice of cork, he found it divided into small compartments and called them cells — the word biology still uses.
body:
Part of [The Scientific Revolution](event:scientific-revolution). *Micrographia* was the Royal Society's first popular success: a large illustrated book with fold-out engravings drawn by Hooke himself of a flea, a louse, the compound eye of a fly, and the point of a needle looking blunt and ragged under magnification. Samuel Pepys sat up until two in the morning with it and called it the most ingenious book he had ever read.

The cork observation was of dead plant tissue: what Hooke saw were the empty walls left behind by cells, and he named them for their likeness to the cells of a monastery. He did not suppose they were the units of life. That idea came in the 1830s with Schleiden and Schwann, and later Virchow, and it needed the better microscopes of the nineteenth century.

Hooke was the Society's curator of experiments, obliged to produce several demonstrations a week, and worked on springs — the law of elasticity is his — on gravitation, on fossils as remains of once-living things, and on rebuilding London as a surveyor after the fire of 1666. His long quarrel with [Newton](event:newton) over priority in the inverse-square law left him a marginal figure for two centuries.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Hooke).

name: Calculus
summary: The mathematics of change: differentiation, which measures rates, and integration, which accumulates them — and the theorem that the two are inverse operations.
body:
Areas and tangents had been attacked for two thousand years, by Archimedes with exhaustion arguments and by Fermat, Cavalieri and Barrow with methods that worked case by case. What [Newton](item:isaac-newton) and Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz supplied in the 1660s and 1670s was a general calculus: a notation and a set of rules that made the problems routine, and the fundamental theorem linking the two operations.

Newton developed his fluxions first and used them in the *[Principia](item:newton)*, though he presented the results there in classical geometry. Leibniz published first, and his notation — dx, dy and the integral sign — is the one still in use. The priority dispute between them, and between their national followers, was long and unedifying.

The foundations were shaky for a century and a half: infinitesimals were quantities that had to be non-zero and then zero, an objection Bishop Berkeley put memorably. Cauchy and Weierstrass replaced them with limits in the nineteenth century. Meanwhile the calculus had become the language of physics and engineering — the [Scientific Revolution's](item:scientific-revolution) most durable instrument, and the basis of every differential equation used to describe a continuous process.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calculus).

name: Leeuwenhoek's microscopes reveal microorganisms
summary: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, a draper in Delft, made single-lens microscopes that magnified up to about 270 times and used them from 1674 to describe protozoa, bacteria, sperm cells and red blood cells — a living world nobody had known was there.
body:
Part of [The Scientific Revolution](event:scientific-revolution). His instruments were not the compound microscopes [Hooke](event:hooke-cells) used but small brass plates holding a single tiny, almost spherical lens, with the specimen mounted on a pin in front of it. They were awkward to use and better than anything else for a century and a half. He ground and mounted the lenses himself and never disclosed his best method; of the several hundred he made, about a dozen survive.

In 1674 he reported "animalcules" swimming in lake water. In 1676 he described much smaller ones — bacteria — in an infusion of pepper and in scrapings from his own teeth. He also described spermatozoa, the banding of striated muscle, yeast cells, and blood corpuscles passing single file through capillaries, which supplied the link [Harvey](event:harvey-circulation) had been unable to see.

He had no Latin and no university training and wrote in Dutch, sending some 190 letters to the Royal Society in London. His claims were so implausible that the Society sent independent observers to verify them before electing him a fellow in 1680. Nothing connected the creatures he found to disease until [germ theory](event:germ-theory), two centuries later.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antonie_van_Leeuwenhoek).

name: Christopher Wren builds St. Paul's Cathedral
summary: Christopher Wren designed a new St Paul's Cathedral after the Great Fire of London destroyed the medieval church in 1666. It was built between 1675 and 1711, and its dome has been a defining image of the city ever since.
body:
Wren was an astronomer and mathematician, a founder of the Royal Society, who turned to architecture in his thirties. His first designs for St Paul's were rejected: the Great Model of 1673, a centralised Greek cross, offended clergy who wanted a long nave for processions. The warrant design he was finally granted he then altered extensively under a clause allowing him to make "ornamental" changes as he went, which is how the built church came to differ so much from the approved drawings.

The dome is the engineering. There are three shells: an inner one shaped for the view from the floor, a brick cone in the middle that carries the stone lantern, and a timber-and-lead outer dome for the skyline, with an iron chain around the base to take the outward thrust. The stone is Portland, shipped from Dorset. Wren was paid partly from a duty on coal entering London, and he lived to see it finished, being hauled up in a basket to inspect the work in his old age.

He also designed fifty-one City parish churches after the fire, whose varied steeples gave London its skyline, and worked at Greenwich, Chelsea and Hampton Court. He is buried in the crypt of St Paul's beneath an inscription that tells the reader who seeks his monument to look around.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Paul%27s_Cathedral).

name: Peter the Great modernizes Russia
summary: Peter I ruled Russia from 1682 to 1725 and forced on it a programme of Western-style reform: a navy, a modern army, a reorganised state and church, and a new capital at St Petersburg. He defeated Sweden and made Russia a European great power.
body:
Peter travelled to the Dutch Republic and England in 1697–98 with a "Grand Embassy", working in shipyards under a thin pretence of anonymity to learn the trade. He came home to crush a revolt of the streltsy, the old Moscow guard, with torture and mass public executions, and then set about remaking the state: a Table of Ranks tying noble status to service rather than birth, new provincial governments, a Senate, administrative colleges on the Swedish model, and the abolition of the patriarchate in favour of a synod under a lay official. He taxed almost everything, beards included.

The Great Northern War against Sweden ran from 1700 to 1721. Beaten at Narva at the outset, he rebuilt the army around conscription and artillery and won decisively at Poltava in 1709; the Treaty of Nystad gave Russia the eastern Baltic coast, and he took the title of emperor. His campaigns against the Ottomans went much less well.

[St Petersburg](event:st-petersburg-founded), begun in 1703 on captured marshland, became the capital in 1712 and was built with conscripted labour at heavy cost in lives. The reforms were imposed from above and paid for by a peasantry whose serfdom deepened under them; his son Alexei died under interrogation for opposing them. Russia after him was a European power organised for war.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_the_Great).

name: Ottoman siege of Vienna
summary: An Ottoman army besieged Vienna from July 1683. On 12 September a relief force led by John III Sobieski of Poland broke the siege in a battle outside the city. It was the last Ottoman attempt on Vienna and the beginning of a long retreat from central Europe.
body:
Part of [Ottoman Empire](event:ottoman-empire). The grand vizier Kara Mustafa Pasha brought perhaps 100,000 men up the Danube. The emperor Leopold I left the city, whose garrison of about 15,000 under Ernst Rüdiger von Starhemberg held walls that Ottoman sappers mined steadily from trenches driven up to the ditch. By early September the defences were breached in places, the food was gone and dysentery was spreading.

A relief army assembled under a treaty between Leopold and Poland-Lithuania, brokered and part-funded by Pope Innocent XI: Polish, Saxon, Bavarian and imperial contingents, about 70,000 men, with Sobieski in overall command. They came down from the wooded Kahlenberg heights north-west of the city on 12 September and fought their way through the Ottoman flank. The action ended with what is usually described as the largest cavalry charge in history, some 18,000 horse including the Polish winged hussars, and the Ottoman camp was taken. Kara Mustafa was executed at Belgrade on the sultan's orders that December.

A Holy League followed up the victory and took Hungary over the next fifteen years. The Treaty of Karlowitz in 1699 was the first in which the Ottomans ceded substantial territory, and Austria became the dominant power in central Europe.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Vienna).

name: J.S. Bach's compositions
summary: Johann Sebastian Bach worked as an organist, court musician and church cantor in provincial Germany and wrote well over a thousand pieces. He is generally regarded as the summit of baroque music, though his reputation came a century after his death.
body:
Bach was born at Eisenach into a family that had supplied musicians to Thuringia for generations, and held posts at Arnstadt, Weimar and Cöthen before becoming Cantor of the Thomasschule in Leipzig in 1723, where he stayed for the rest of his life. The Leipzig job required new music for most Sundays of the church year: he wrote some 300 cantatas, of which about 200 survive, along with the *St Matthew* and *St John* Passions and the Mass in B minor.

The instrumental music was often written for teaching or for a particular employer — the *Brandenburg Concertos*, offered to a margrave who seems never to have had them played; the *Well-Tempered Clavier*, two sets of preludes and fugues in all twenty-four keys; the cello suites; the *Goldberg Variations*; and *The Art of Fugue*, left unfinished. The technique is contrapuntal: several independent voices, each a melody, which together make the harmony. He never travelled outside Germany.

In his lifetime he was known chiefly as an organ virtuoso, and by the time he died in 1750 his style was thought old-fashioned. Mendelssohn's performance of the *St Matthew Passion* in 1829 began the revival, and a complete edition followed later in the century.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johann_Sebastian_Bach).

name: The Enlightenment
summary: The Enlightenment was an intellectual movement of the long eighteenth century which held that reason, evidence and free criticism should decide any claim, whether about nature, religion or government. It ran from roughly the 1680s to the end of the century, centred on France, Britain, Scotland and the German states.
body:
Its confidence came from the [new science](event:scientific-revolution): if the heavens obeyed laws that a person could work out, so might society. Locke argued that knowledge comes from experience and that government rests on consent and may be dissolved; [Montesquieu](event:montesquieu-spirit) analysed how power might be divided so that it checks itself; [Voltaire](event:voltaire-enlightenment) attacked judicial cruelty, censorship and clerical privilege; [Hume](event:hume-philosophy) pressed empiricism to sceptical conclusions; [Rousseau](event:rousseau-social) dissented from much of it, holding that civilisation corrupts; [Adam Smith](event:wealth-of-nations) described a commercial society ordered without anyone directing it; Kant answered the question "what is enlightenment?" with a motto — dare to know.

It was carried by print and by sociability rather than by universities: the [*Encyclopédie*](event:diderot-encyclopedia), pamphlets, cheap pirated reprints, coffee houses, Parisian salons run by women, provincial academies and masonic lodges. Much of it was printed abroad or clandestinely to evade the censors. Beccaria's argument against torture and the death penalty, and the campaign against the [slave trade](event:slave-trade), show what it produced in practice.

Its politics were not uniform: some looked to reforming monarchs ([enlightened absolutism](event:enlightened-despotism)), others to representative government. Its language of natural rights and popular sovereignty passed into the [American](event:american-revolution) and [French](event:french-revolution) revolutions. Critics from the Romantics onward charged it with a thin view of tradition, feeling and community, and with a universalism that in practice excluded women, the poor and the colonised.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Age_of_Enlightenment).

name: Newton's Principia
summary: Isaac Newton's *Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica*, published in 1687, set out three laws of motion and a law of universal gravitation. A single set of principles accounted for falling bodies, the tides, the paths of comets and the orbits of the planets.
body:
Part of [The Scientific Revolution](event:scientific-revolution). The book was written in about eighteen months after Edmond Halley asked [Newton](item:isaac-newton) what curve a planet would follow under an inverse-square attraction and was told, from memory, an ellipse — Newton had worked it out years earlier and mislaid the proof. Halley paid for the printing himself.

The first law says a body keeps its state of rest or uniform motion unless a force acts on it; the second relates force to change of motion; the third pairs every action with an equal and opposite reaction. Gravitation is universal: every mass attracts every other in proportion to the product of the masses and inversely as the square of the distance between them. From these Newton derived [Kepler's laws](event:kepler), explained the tides by the pull of Moon and Sun, showed why the Earth bulges at the equator, and made comets predictable — a prediction Halley's comet kept in 1758.

The argument is presented in classical geometry rather than in the [calculus](item:calculus) Newton had invented and used, which is one reason the book is so hard. He declined to say what gravity *is* — *hypotheses non fingo*, I feign no hypotheses — and gave only the law by which it acts, an omission Continental followers of Descartes attacked for decades as a return to occult qualities. The *Principia* set the standard the sciences aimed at for two hundred years, until [relativity](event:relativity) showed the limits of its account of gravity without displacing it as a working theory.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philosophiæ_Naturalis_Principia_Mathematica).

name: Glorious Revolution
summary: In November 1688 William of Orange landed in England at the invitation of leading politicians, and James II fled to France. Parliament declared the throne vacant, made William and Mary joint monarchs, and passed a Bill of Rights that fixed the limits of royal power.
body:
James II was Catholic, and had been tolerated on the expectation that his Protestant daughter Mary would succeed him. He suspended penal laws by prerogative, placed Catholics in the army, the universities and the government, and prosecuted seven bishops who petitioned against him. The birth of a son in June 1688 promised a Catholic dynasty instead, and seven peers and bishops wrote to William — Mary's husband and the Dutch stadtholder — inviting him to intervene.

William crossed with a large fleet and about 15,000 troops. James's army melted away, his nerve failed, and he was deliberately allowed to escape, which let Parliament treat the throne as abandoned rather than seized. The settlement of 1689 required the monarch to be Protestant, forbade a standing army or taxation without parliamentary consent, guaranteed frequent elections and free speech in Parliament, and barred the suspending of laws. A Toleration Act gave Protestant dissenters freedom of worship.

It was neither bloodless nor purely English. It brought England into William's war against Louis XIV, which required regular parliaments to vote money and led to the Bank of England in 1694 and a permanent funded national debt. In Ireland and Scotland it was decided by fighting — the Boyne in 1690 — and left a Jacobite cause that lasted until 1746.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glorious_Revolution).

name: Voltaire's philosophy and writings
summary: Voltaire was the most widely read French writer of the eighteenth century and the Enlightenment's most effective polemicist. He attacked religious intolerance, censorship and judicial cruelty in poems, plays, histories, letters and short satirical tales.
body:
Part of [The Enlightenment](event:enlightenment). Born François-Marie Arouet, he was imprisoned in the Bastille at twenty-two for verses against the regent, and later beaten by a nobleman's servants and exiled for answering back. Two and a half years in England left him an admirer of its religious toleration, its constitution and [Newton](event:newton), whose physics he did much to popularise in France; his *Lettres philosophiques* of 1734 used English practice as a rebuke to French, and was burned by the public hangman.

He wrote tragedies, an epic, a history of the age of Louis XIV, an *Essay on Customs* that took in China and the Islamic world, and articles for the [*Encyclopédie*](event:diderot-encyclopedia). *Candide* (1759) mocked the doctrine that this is the best of all possible worlds, a target sharpened by the [Lisbon earthquake](event:lisbon-earthquake).

From Ferney, an estate near the Swiss border he could cross if the police came, he ran campaigns for the victims of judicial persecution — above all Jean Calas, a Protestant broken on the wheel in 1762 on a false charge of murdering his son, whose conviction Voltaire got quashed posthumously. *Écrasez l'infâme* — crush the infamous thing — meant clerical and judicial persecution rather than religion as such: he was a deist, and no democrat.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voltaire).

name: Founding of St. Petersburg
summary: Peter the Great founded St Petersburg in May 1703 on marshland at the mouth of the Neva, on ground just taken from Sweden. It became the Russian capital in 1712 and remained so until 1918.
body:
Part of [Peter the Great](event:peter-the-great)'s remaking of Russia. The site was chosen for access to the Baltic, not for comfort: flat, flooded, freezing, with no stone and no local labour. Tens of thousands of conscripted peasants, soldiers and Swedish prisoners were sent north each year to drive piles and dig canals, and large numbers died of disease, cold and exhaustion — the city has been called one built on bones, though the figures are not documented.

Peter had it laid out on a European plan by Italian, French and German architects: straight avenues, granite embankments, the Peter and Paul Fortress, the Admiralty shipyard, and later the Winter Palace. Nobles were ordered to build houses there and merchants to trade through the port, and stone building was banned elsewhere in Russia for a time so that masons would have to come.

It was Russia's window on the West, its chief port and the seat of its court, and by 1900 one of the largest cities in Europe and the centre of its literature, music and revolutionary politics. It was renamed Petrograd in 1914, Leningrad in 1924, and St Petersburg again in 1991.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Petersburg).

name: Act of Union creates Great Britain
summary: The Acts of Union passed by the English and Scottish parliaments in 1706 and 1707 joined the two kingdoms into one, called Great Britain, with a single parliament at Westminster from 1 May 1707.
body:
The crowns had been shared since James VI of Scotland inherited the English throne in 1603, but the kingdoms kept separate parliaments, and by 1700 the arrangement was breaking down. Scotland's parliament asserted a right to choose a different successor to Queen Anne; England, at war with France, could not accept a separate Scottish foreign policy on its northern border. The failure of the Darién scheme, a Scottish attempt at a colony in Panama that swallowed a large share of the country's liquid capital, made access to English colonial markets attractive to those who had lost money — and the compensation fund written into the treaty, the *Equivalent*, went largely to them.

The treaty gave Scotland 45 seats in the Commons and 16 elected peers in the Lords, free trade within the union and its empire, and the retention of its own legal system, courts, burghs and Presbyterian church. It was unpopular in the streets of Edinburgh and Glasgow and was carried in the Scottish parliament by a majority its opponents said had been bought; Burns later wrote of a nation "bought and sold for English gold".

The union held. Jacobite risings in 1715 and 1745 failed to undo it, and Scots took a large part in British trade, empire, science and the Enlightenment that followed. Scottish independence was rejected in a referendum in 2014.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acts_of_Union_1707).

name: Yongzheng Emperor's Qing reforms
summary: The Yongzheng Emperor ruled the Qing for thirteen years from 1722. He centralised decision-making, attacked corruption, reformed the tax system and left a full treasury — the administrative link between his father Kangxi's conquests and his son Qianlong's long prosperity.
body:
Part of [Qing dynasty](event:qing-dynasty). He came to the throne in disputed circumstances after the long succession struggle among [Kangxi](event:kangxi-emperor)'s sons, and dealt with his surviving brothers harshly, imprisoning several. He worked prodigiously, reading and annotating memorials late into the night in his own hand.

The palace memorial system let chosen officials write to the emperor directly and in secret, bypassing the bureaucracy that would otherwise have edited the report — an intelligence channel that made provincial governors individually accountable. He created what became the Grand Council, a small inner body for urgent business. He merged the head tax into the land tax, so that liability fell on land rather than on people, and legalised a surcharge that had long been collected informally, using it to pay officials a "salary to nourish honesty" instead of leaving them to live on fees. He also freed several hereditary outcast groups from their debased legal status.

In the south-west he replaced hereditary native chieftains with regular officials, at the cost of years of fighting. The scholar-elite whose latitude he curtailed disliked him, and his historical reputation suffered accordingly; the state he handed on in 1735 was solvent and tightly run.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongzheng_Emperor).

name: Hume's empiricist philosophy
summary: David Hume, a Scottish philosopher and historian, argued that all knowledge comes from experience, and pressed the argument to sceptical conclusions: that causation is a habit of expectation rather than something observed, and that reason alone cannot tell anyone what to do.
body:
Part of [The Enlightenment](event:enlightenment). *A Treatise of Human Nature* appeared in 1739–40, when Hume was in his twenties, and in his own words "fell dead-born from the press". He recast its arguments in the *Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding* (1748) and the *Enquiry Concerning the Principles of Morals* (1751), which he thought his best work.

Three arguments have kept their force. On induction: no amount of past regularity gives a logical reason to expect the future to resemble it, so the expectation rests on custom rather than on proof. On causation: we observe one event constantly following another and never a necessary connection between them. On is and ought: a conclusion about what ought to be done cannot be derived from premises stating only what is, which Hume noted in a single paragraph that has been argued over ever since. He also denied that we have any impression of a continuing self, and in the posthumous *Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion* dismantled the argument from design.

He was refused chairs at Edinburgh and Glasgow on suspicion of atheism and made his living as a librarian, diplomat and author of a best-selling *History of England*. Kant said Hume woke him from dogmatic slumber, and much of empiricism since has been a series of answers to his problems.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Hume).

name: Enlightened despotism in Prussia and Austria
summary: Several eighteenth-century monarchs — Frederick II of Prussia, Maria Theresa and Joseph II of Austria, Catherine II of Russia — adopted Enlightenment ideas about law, toleration and administration while keeping absolute power. The pattern is usually called enlightened absolutism.
body:
Part of [The Enlightenment](event:enlightenment). Frederick took the throne in 1740, invaded Silesia within months, and spent much of his reign at war. He also abolished judicial torture, allowed broad religious toleration and a relatively free press, began the codification of Prussian law, and corresponded with [Voltaire](event:voltaire-enlightenment), who stayed three years at Potsdam before the friendship collapsed. Frederick called himself the first servant of the state.

Maria Theresa reformed taxation, the army and the central administration out of necessity after losing Silesia, and made primary schooling compulsory in 1774. Her son Joseph II went furthest and fastest: he abolished serfdom, issued a Patent of Toleration for Protestants, Orthodox and Jews, dissolved contemplative monasteries and used their funds for parishes and hospitals, imposed German as the language of administration everywhere, and legislated a single code. Almost all of it provoked revolt in Hungary and the Netherlands, and most was withdrawn at his death in 1790.

The reforms were made from above, in the interest of a stronger state as much as a freer subject: censorship, serfdom in Prussia and Russia, and noble privilege survived wherever they were useful. The phrase "everything for the people, nothing by the people" is a later summary of the position. The [French Revolution](event:french-revolution) exposed the tension, and most of these governments turned to repression afterwards.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enlightened_absolutism).

name: Montesquieu's separation of powers
summary: Montesquieu's *The Spirit of the Laws*, published in 1748, argued that political liberty is preserved by dividing government into legislative, executive and judicial powers that check one another. It was among the most influential political books of the century.
body:
Part of [The Enlightenment](event:enlightenment). Charles-Louis de Secondat, baron de Montesquieu, was a magistrate in Bordeaux who sold his office and spent twenty years on the book after travelling in Europe, including nearly two years in England. He had already made his name with the *Persian Letters* (1721), a satire of French society written in the voice of two Persian visitors.

The argument is comparative. Laws are not deduced from first principles but grow out of a people's climate, terrain, religion, commerce and manners — the "spirit" of the title — so that what suits one nation may ruin another. He classified governments as republics, monarchies and despotisms, each animated by its own principle: virtue, honour, fear. His model of separated powers was drawn from a reading of the English constitution that misdescribed it in places, and it was the reading rather than the reality that mattered.

The book was placed on the Index and went through many editions anyway. The framers of the [United States Constitution](event:us-constitution) cited him more than any other modern author. His climatic explanations of national character, and his equivocation on slavery — the famous chapter is ironic, and was read straight by some — have worn much less well.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montesquieu).

name: Diderot's Encyclopédie
summary: The *Encyclopédie*, edited by Denis Diderot with Jean le Rond d'Alembert, appeared in Paris between 1751 and 1772: seventeen volumes of text and eleven of plates, some 72,000 articles by around 140 contributors. It was the great collective work of the Enlightenment.
body:
Part of [The Enlightenment](event:enlightenment). It began as a translation of an English cyclopedia and became something else: a survey of knowledge organised not by revelation but by the faculties of the human mind, with a system of cross-references that let a cautious article on an orthodox subject point the reader to a sceptical one elsewhere. Contributors included [Voltaire](event:voltaire-enlightenment), [Rousseau](event:rousseau-social), Montesquieu, Turgot and Quesnay; d'Alembert wrote the preliminary discourse and withdrew in 1759 under pressure.

Its treatment of the mechanical arts was deliberate and unusual. Diderot visited workshops, questioned craftsmen and had their tools and processes engraved in detail, on the argument that what a glassblower or a stocking-frame knitter knows deserves the same standing as what a bishop knows.

The privilege to publish was revoked in 1759 and the work continued semi-clandestinely with official knowledge; Diderot discovered late that his own publisher had been censoring the sheets behind his back. About 4,000 sets were sold before cheaper foreign reprints spread it much further. It made a body of critical, secular knowledge available to anyone who could afford a subscription, which is precisely what its enemies objected to.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Encyclopédie).

name: Konbaung Dynasty unites Burma
summary: Alaungpaya founded the Konbaung dynasty in 1752 and reunified Burma after the collapse of the previous kingdom. Its rulers carried Burmese power to its greatest extent, and it was the last Burmese dynasty, ending with British annexation in 1885.
body:
The Restored Toungoo kingdom fell in 1752 to a rebellion from Lower Burma that took the capital at Ava. Alaungpaya, headman of a village near Shwebo, refused to submit, gathered a following, retook the country within five years, and destroyed the rival capital at Pegu in 1757. He founded Rangoon on the site of a fishing village near the mouth of the Irrawaddy.

His successors invaded Siam and sacked Ayutthaya in 1767, and between 1765 and 1769 fought off four invasions sent by the Qianlong Emperor. That war, expensive and unsuccessful for the Qing, was decided as much by malaria in the frontier hills as by battle. Later campaigns took Arakan in 1785 and Manipur and Assam in the following decades, carrying the Burmese frontier up to British Bengal.

That contact proved fatal. Three Anglo-Burmese wars — 1824–26, 1852 and 1885 — took first the coastal provinces, then Lower Burma, then the rest; the first was among the most expensive wars the East India Company ever fought. King Thibaw was deported to India in 1885 and Burma became a province of British India.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Konbaung_Dynasty).

name: Lisbon earthquake
summary: An earthquake estimated at magnitude 8.5 or more struck off the Portuguese coast on the morning of 1 November 1755, All Saints' Day. Shaking, a tsunami and fire destroyed most of Lisbon and killed tens of thousands of people.
body:
The shock came in several pulses over some minutes and opened fissures in the city centre. Survivors ran for the open ground of the waterfront; about forty minutes later the sea withdrew from the harbour and returned as a wave several metres high. Fires started by cooking hearths and by the candles lit in churches full for the feast day burned for days in what the water had not reached. Estimates of the dead in Lisbon range from about 12,000 to 50,000, and the tsunami also killed people in southern Portugal, Spain and Morocco.

The king's minister, later Marquis of Pombal, took charge with the instruction to bury the dead and feed the living. He hanged looters and rebuilt the lower town on a grid of standardised buildings framed in timber cages designed to flex — an early attempt at earthquake-resistant construction. He also circulated a questionnaire to every parish asking how long the shaking lasted, which way it ran, and how the wells and the sea behaved; the returns are a founding document of seismology.

The disaster struck a devout capital on a holy day, and forced the problem of evil into public argument. [Voltaire](event:voltaire-enlightenment) answered it in a poem and again in *Candide*; Rousseau replied that the deaths owed something to the decision to build seven storeys high.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1755_Lisbon_earthquake).

name: Mozart's compositions
summary: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart composed more than 600 works in thirty-five years — symphonies, concertos, operas, chamber and sacred music — and is one of the central figures of the classical style.
body:
He was a prodigy, exhibited across Europe by his father Leopold from the age of six, playing for courts in Munich, Paris, London and Vienna and absorbing every national style he met. He wrote his first symphony at eight and his first opera at eleven, and spent his twenties chafing at a post in Salzburg under an archbishop he detested, until he was dismissed in 1781 — with a kick, by his own account — and settled in Vienna.

There he worked freelance on subscription concerts, pupils, publication and commissions, which brought him a considerable income and no security at all. The mature work includes the last symphonies, numbers 39 to 41; the piano concertos he wrote to play himself; the six string quartets dedicated to Haydn, whom he admired and who admired him; and the operas — *The Marriage of Figaro*, *Don Giovanni*, *Così fan tutte* and *The Magic Flute*, the first three to librettos by Lorenzo da Ponte.

He died in Vienna in December 1791, probably of an infectious illness, leaving the Requiem unfinished and debts his widow took years to clear. He was buried in a common grave, which was ordinary for the time and place; the story that Salieri poisoned him is a later legend. His work is the reference point of the classical style.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wolfgang_Amadeus_Mozart).

name: Seven Years' War
summary: The Seven Years' War was fought from 1756 to 1763 in Europe, North America, the Caribbean, West Africa, India and the Philippines. Britain and Prussia faced France, Austria, Russia and later Spain. Britain emerged with Canada and dominance in India; France lost most of its overseas empire.
body:
The alignment was new. Britain had been allied with Austria and France with Prussia; after the diplomatic revolution of 1756 the pairs swapped, and Austria set out to recover Silesia, which Frederick II of Prussia had seized in the previous war. Frederick struck first into Saxony. Fighting in North America had already begun in 1754, where the conflict is called the French and Indian War.

In Europe Prussia survived by interior lines, hard marching and Frederick's victories at Rossbach and Leuthen in 1757, and by British subsidies. It came close to collapse by 1761 and was saved when the Russian empress Elizabeth died and her successor, an admirer of Frederick, left the war. Overseas, sea power decided matters: Quebec fell in 1759, Montreal in 1760, the French posts in India by 1761, and Havana and Manila in 1762 after Spain entered.

The Peace of Paris in 1763 gave Britain Canada, Florida and predominance in India, where [Plassey](event:battle-plassey) had already put Bengal under the [East India Company](event:english-east-india). The Treaty of Hubertusburg restored the German boundaries and confirmed Prussia as a great power. Britain's war debt led it to tax its American colonies, and France's defeat and expense fed both its support for the [American Revolution](event:american-revolution) and the fiscal crisis behind the [French Revolution](event:french-revolution). It is often described as the first global war.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seven_Years%27_War).

steps.name: Minorca and the invasion of Saxony
steps.page:
France opened the European war by taking Minorca in May 1756; the British admiral who failed to relieve it, John Byng, was court-martialled and shot on his own quarterdeck.

Frederick II struck first on land, marching into neutral Saxony in August, forcing the Saxon army to capitulate in October and pressing its soldiers into his own. The invasion gave his enemies a casus belli and gave him a base and a treasury.

steps.name: Rossbach and Leuthen
steps.page:
1757 nearly finished Prussia: Frederick was beaten at Kolín and invaded from three directions. Then in five weeks he destroyed a Franco-imperial army at Rossbach in November, marching his infantry across the enemy front, and an Austrian army twice his size at Leuthen in December.

Leuthen was fought by an oblique advance against one flank on ground he had drilled on in peacetime. The two victories kept Prussia in the war and made his military reputation across Europe.

steps.name: The year of victories
steps.page:
British and allied arms won everywhere in the second half of 1759. Minden in August stopped the French in Germany; Lagos and then Quiberon Bay in November wrecked the two French fleets and ended any prospect of invading Britain.

On 13 September Wolfe's army scaled the cliffs above Quebec and beat Montcalm on the Plains of Abraham; both commanders were killed, and the city surrendered days later. Montreal followed in 1760, ending French rule in Canada.

steps.name: Prussia's crisis and the Russian withdrawal
steps.page:
By 1761 Frederick had lost Silesian fortresses, Russian and Austrian armies had burned Berlin, his best troops were dead and Britain had stopped his subsidy. He carried poison and expected the end.

The Empress Elizabeth died in January 1762 and was succeeded by Peter III, an admirer who at once made peace and returned every conquest — the reversal Prussian historians called the miracle of the House of Brandenburg.

steps.name: Spain enters: Havana and Manila
steps.page:
Spain joined France in 1762 and lost two of its great colonial ports within months. A British expedition took Havana in August after a siege in which disease killed far more of the attackers than the fighting did.

A second force from Madras took Manila in October. Both were handed back at the peace — Havana in exchange for Florida — but the ease of their capture was noted everywhere.

steps.name: The Peace of Paris and Hubertusburg
steps.page:
By the Treaty of Paris on 10 February 1763 France ceded Canada and its territory east of the Mississippi to Britain, kept its sugar islands and its fishing rights, and abandoned political ambitions in India. Spain gave up Florida and received Louisiana from France.

Five days later the Treaty of Hubertusburg restored the German boundaries exactly as they had been: Prussia kept Silesia, Austria kept its dignity, and eight years of war had changed nothing in central Europe except the reputation of the Prussian army.

name: Battle of Plassey
summary: On 23 June 1757 an East India Company force under Robert Clive defeated Siraj ud-Daulah, Nawab of Bengal, at Plassey north of Calcutta. The battle put Bengal under Company control and began British territorial rule in India.
body:
The quarrel began when the young nawab took Calcutta in 1756, an episode remembered in Britain for the deaths of prisoners held overnight in the so-called Black Hole. Clive retook the city with a force from Madras. What followed was less a battle than the execution of a conspiracy: Clive, the Bengali banking house of Jagat Seth and other merchants had already agreed with Mir Jafar, the nawab's own commander, that he would hold back and be made nawab in his place.

Clive had about 3,000 men, two-thirds of them Indian sepoys, against perhaps 50,000. An afternoon rainstorm soaked the nawab's powder while the Company's guns, covered with tarpaulins, went on firing; Mir Jafar's large contingent never engaged. The fighting lasted a few hours and cost the Company around twenty dead. Siraj ud-Daulah fled and was killed days later.

Mir Jafar paid for his throne with enormous sums to the Company and to its officers individually; Clive took a personal fortune and was questioned about it in Parliament years afterwards. Victory at Buxar in 1764 confirmed the position, and in 1765 the Company obtained the *diwani*, the right to collect Bengal's revenue. From then the [Company](event:english-east-india) governed as well as traded.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Plassey).

name: Industrial Revolution
summary: From about 1760 Britain began making goods with machines driven by water and then by coal-fired steam, in factories rather than in households. Output per worker rose faster than population for the first time in history, and the pattern spread to western Europe, North America and eventually the world.
body:
Textiles came first, because spinning was the bottleneck: [the jenny, the water frame and the mule](event:spinning-jenny) multiplied what one worker could produce, and the work moved to where the power was. [Watt's engine](event:watt-engine), with its separate condenser and later its rotary drive, freed factories from riverbanks. Coke smelting and Cort's puddling process made cheap wrought iron; canals and then [railways](event:railways) carried coal, iron and cloth at a fraction of the old cost. Britain had the coal, the shipping, the colonial markets, the patent law and the capital, and historians still argue about which of those mattered most.

The social consequences arrived faster than any means of handling them. Manchester's population multiplied several times over in fifty years, into housing without drains or clean water, and life expectancy in the industrial towns was lower than in the countryside they drew on. Work was disciplined by the clock and the machine rather than by daylight and season. Children worked in mills and mines until the Factory Acts began restricting it from 1833. Handloom weavers were ruined; the Luddites broke frames in 1811–13; trade unions, the Chartist movement and a new vocabulary of class all came out of the same decades.

The change was not only economic. Sustained growth in output per head, energy use, urbanisation and population all begin their steep rise here, and so does the atmospheric carbon dioxide behind [modern climate change](event:global-warming). It is the deepest break in how human beings live since agriculture.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Industrial_Revolution).

steps.name: Cromford and the factory system
steps.page:
Richard Arkwright's mill at Cromford, opened in 1771, ran water-powered frames day and night with a workforce of several hundred, many of them children, housed in a village built for them.

The machine was only half the invention. The other half was the organisation: fixed hours, shifts, supervision and a discipline of the clock that had no precedent in the domestic workshops it replaced.

steps.name: Cheap iron: coke, puddling and the first iron bridge
steps.page:
Abraham Darby's family had smelted iron with coke rather than charcoal at Coalbrookdale since 1709, breaking the dependence on woodland. In 1779 the third Darby cast the world's first iron bridge over the Severn there.

Henry Cort's puddling and rolling process, patented in 1783–84, made wrought iron from pig iron with coal rather than charcoal and at many times the rate. Cheap iron made everything else — machines, rails, boilers, ships — possible.

steps.name: Steam-powered cotton and the mule
steps.page:
The first Boulton and Watt rotative engine drove a cotton mill at Papplewick in 1785, and steam quickly displaced water in the Lancashire trade because a mill could then be built where the labour and the canal were.

Crompton's mule was scaled up and fitted with steam drive; Cartwright's power loom, patented in 1785, took another two decades to become practical. British raw cotton consumption rose more than tenfold in twenty years.

steps.name: The factory town and the first Factory Acts
steps.page:
By the 1830s the consequences were being counted: cholera in 1832, Chadwick's sanitary inquiry, and evidence to parliamentary commissions about children working twelve-hour days in mills and hauling in mines.

The Factory Act of 1833 limited children's hours in textile mills and, for the first time, appointed inspectors to enforce it. The Mines Act of 1842 followed. Neither went far, and both established that the state would regulate what went on inside a private factory.

name: Rousseau's The Social Contract
summary: Jean-Jacques Rousseau's *The Social Contract* (1762) opens with the claim that man is born free and is everywhere in chains, and argues that a legitimate state is one in which citizens obey only laws they have made themselves, expressing a 'general will'.
body:
Part of [The Enlightenment](event:enlightenment). Rousseau was a Genevan watchmaker's son who had reached his position in two earlier discourses: that the arts and sciences had corrupted morals rather than improved them, and that inequality originates in property and in the institutions built to protect it. He is the Enlightenment's great internal critic, and he quarrelled in turn with [Voltaire](event:voltaire-enlightenment), with Diderot and with Hume.

The contract in his account is not a bargain trading freedom for security, as in Hobbes, but the act by which a people constitutes itself as a people. Sovereignty then stays with the whole body of citizens and cannot be represented or delegated; a government is only its agent and may be dismissed. The general will is what citizens will as citizens, which is not the sum of what they severally want — the phrase that has done the most work and the most damage, since a ruler claiming to know it can claim to force people to be free, which the text does say.

*Émile*, on education, appeared the same year; both books were condemned in Paris and Geneva and Rousseau spent years moving between refuges. His *Confessions* invented a kind of self-examination the Romantics took up wholesale. The Jacobins made him a patron of the [French Revolution](event:french-revolution) and moved his remains to the Panthéon in 1794.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Social_Contract).

name: Mechanised spinning
summary: Between 1764 and 1779 three machines — Hargreaves's spinning jenny, Arkwright's water frame and Crompton's mule — broke the bottleneck in making yarn. Spinning moved out of the cottage and into the mill, and the factory system began with it.
body:
Part of [Industrial Revolution](event:industrial-revolution). Under the old arrangement it took several hand spinners to keep one weaver supplied, and Kay's flying shuttle of 1733 had made the weaver faster still. James Hargreaves's jenny, built about 1764, let one worker turn eight spindles at once and eventually many more; its yarn was soft and could be used only as weft.

Richard Arkwright's water frame, patented in 1769, drew the fibre through rollers turning at different speeds and produced thread strong enough for warp, so that cloth could be made of cotton throughout. It was too large and too power-hungry for a house, so Arkwright built mills — at Cromford from 1771, water-driven, employing whole families on shifts around the clock, which is as much the invention as the machine. Samuel Crompton's mule of 1779 combined both principles and spun fine, strong yarn; steam-driven mules later carried over a thousand spindles each.

British cotton output rose enormously and cheap cloth was exported worldwide, undercutting Indian handloom weaving in India itself. The demand for raw cotton was met by slave plantations in the American south. Hargreaves's neighbours are said to have broken into his house and smashed his machines — the first of a long series of such episodes.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spinning_jenny).

name: Napoleon Bonaparte
summary: French general who made himself emperor, dominated Europe for a decade, and left behind a legal code still in use across much of the world.
body:
Born on Corsica a year after France annexed it, Napoleon was trained at French military schools and made his name in the artillery during [the Revolution](item:french-revolution). Command in Italy and an expedition to Egypt built his reputation; in 1799 he [seized power](item:napoleon-coup) in a coup, and in 1804 crowned himself emperor.

As a commander he moved armies faster than his opponents could react and concentrated force at the decisive point; [Austerlitz](item:austerlitz) in 1805 is the usual textbook example. [The wars](item:napoleonic-wars) that carry his name put most of Europe under French control or influence, but Britain held the sea after [Trafalgar](item:trafalgar), Spain became an unwinnable guerrilla war, and [the invasion of Russia](item:russia-1812) in 1812 destroyed the Grande Armée. He abdicated in 1814, returned for a hundred days, and was beaten at [Waterloo](item:waterloo).

He died in British custody on Saint Helena. The Napoleonic Code, a centralised administration, the metric system and conscription outlasted him, and the nationalism his campaigns provoked shaped Europe for a century.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Napoleon).

name: Goethe's literary influence
summary: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe was the dominant figure in German literature for half a century — poet, dramatist, novelist, critic, court official and amateur scientist. *The Sorrows of Young Werther* made him famous across Europe in 1774, when he was twenty-four.
body:
*Werther* is a short novel in letters about a young man who kills himself over an unattainable love. It was a sensation: readers dressed in the hero's blue coat and yellow waistcoat, and it was blamed then and afterwards for a wave of imitative suicides. It belonged to *Sturm und Drang*, the movement that set feeling and individual genius against the rules of French classicism.

The Duke of Weimar brought him to court in 1775, and Goethe spent the rest of his life there, running mines, roads and the theatre and sitting on the privy council. A journey to Italy in 1786–88 turned him towards classical restraint. *Wilhelm Meister's Apprenticeship* (1795–96) established the German novel of formation, the *Bildungsroman*, and his lyrics and ballads were set to music by Schubert, Schumann and Wolf. His friendship and correspondence with Schiller shaped both men's work in the 1790s.

*Faust*, begun in his twenties and completed the year before his death in 1832, is the work he is measured by: a scholar's bargain with Mephistopheles that opens in a study and ends, in the second part, as a symbolic drama of the whole modern world. He also wrote on plant morphology and a theory of colour intended to refute [Newton](event:newton), which physicists rejected and painters read with interest.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johann_Wolfgang_von_Goethe).

name: American Revolution
summary: Thirteen British colonies in North America went to war with Britain in 1775, declared independence in 1776 and won recognition of it in 1783. The new United States then wrote a federal constitution — the first modern republic founded on a written statement of natural rights.
body:
The quarrel followed the [Seven Years' War](event:seven-years-war), when Parliament tried to make the colonies pay a share of imperial defence through the Stamp Act, the Townshend duties and the tea tax. Colonists objected that they were being taxed by a body in which they were not represented, and that their own assemblies had long held that power. Boycotts, riots and Britain's coercive response to the destruction of tea in Boston harbour in 1773 hardened both sides, and shooting began at Lexington and Concord in April 1775.

Britain's problem was distance and the absence of a decisive target. Washington's Continental Army had to be kept in being rather than made to win, and it survived Long Island, the loss of New York and Philadelphia and the winter at Valley Forge. Saratoga in 1777 brought France into the war in 1778, followed by Spain and the Dutch Republic, turning a colonial rebellion into a global one that stretched British forces from Gibraltar to India. A French fleet closed the Chesapeake and made [Yorktown](event:yorktown) a surrender rather than a siege that could be relieved.

Perhaps a fifth of the population stayed loyal to the Crown, and some 60,000 left, most for Canada. Native nations, most of which had sided with Britain as the power more likely to restrain settlement, lost their protector in the peace. Slavery survived the language of the [Declaration](event:declaration-independence): northern states began abolishing it, southern states did not, and the question was deferred into the [Constitution](event:us-constitution) and eventually into a civil war. The revolution's example, and the debt France ran up paying for it, contributed to the [French Revolution](event:french-revolution) six years later.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Revolution).

steps.name: Lexington and Concord
steps.page:
British regulars marched out of Boston on the night of 18 April 1775 to seize militia stores at Concord. Riders including Paul Revere raised the countryside ahead of them.

Shots were exchanged on Lexington green at dawn and again at Concord bridge, and the column was fired on from behind walls all the way back to Boston, losing some 270 men. Within weeks a militia army had besieged the city.

steps.name: Saratoga and the French alliance
steps.page:
A British army under Burgoyne moving south from Canada was fought to a standstill at Freeman's Farm and Bemis Heights and surrendered nearly 6,000 men at Saratoga on 17 October 1777.
