It was the first surrender of a British army in the war, and it convinced France that the Americans could win. The treaties of alliance and commerce were signed in Paris on 6 February 1778, turning a colonial rebellion into a European war.

steps.name: The war moves south
steps.page:
Unable to force a decision in the north, Britain turned to the southern colonies, expecting loyalist support. Savannah fell in December 1778 and Charleston in May 1780, with the capture of a whole American army.

What followed was a vicious partisan war of raids and reprisals. Greene's campaign traded ground for time, and Cornwallis, having won at Guilford Court House in March 1781 at ruinous cost, marched into Virginia with an army worn thin.

steps.name: The Treaty of Paris
steps.page:
Negotiations opened in Paris in 1782, with Franklin, Adams and Jay dealing separately with Britain despite the French alliance and getting better terms for it.

The treaty signed on 3 September 1783 recognised the United States as independent and granted a western boundary at the Mississippi — far more than the fighting had won, and made at the expense of the Native nations who had fought as British allies. Britain settled separately with France and Spain the same day.

name: Adam Smith, The Wealth of Nations
summary: Adam Smith's *An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations*, published in 1776, argued that a nation's wealth is the goods its people produce rather than the bullion it holds, and that specialisation and voluntary exchange increase it. It founded economics as a subject.
body:
Part of [The Enlightenment](event:enlightenment). Smith was professor of moral philosophy at Glasgow and had already published *The Theory of Moral Sentiments*, which grounds morality in sympathy — the two books are properly read together, since the later one assumes the earlier one's account of what moves people.

The famous opening describes a pin factory: ten workers who each perform one operation make far more pins than ten working separately, and the extent of that division of labour is limited by the size of the market, which is the case for wide trade. Prices in a competitive market carry information and draw resources where they are wanted; the butcher and the brewer supply dinner from their own interest rather than from benevolence, and are led "as by an invisible hand" to an outcome none of them intended. The phrase occurs once in the book.

Its polemical target was mercantilism — tariffs, chartered monopolies, colonial trade restrictions, and the habit of treating exports as gain and imports as loss. Smith was no apologist for merchants, who in his account seldom meet together without conspiring against the public, and he argued for public works, schooling and taxes falling more than proportionately on the rich. Its arguments shaped nineteenth-century free trade policy.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wealth_of_Nations).

name: Watt's steam engine
summary: James Watt patented a steam engine with a separate condenser in 1769 and, in partnership with Matthew Boulton, began selling engines in 1776. It burned a fraction of the fuel of earlier designs, and once adapted to turn a shaft it could drive machinery anywhere.
body:
Part of [Industrial Revolution](event:industrial-revolution). Thomas Newcomen's atmospheric engine, working since 1712, condensed steam inside the cylinder to make a vacuum, which meant cooling and reheating the whole cylinder on every stroke. It was useful only where fuel was nearly free, at the pithead. Watt, repairing a model of one at Glasgow, saw that condensing in a separate vessel would let the cylinder stay hot; his engines cut coal consumption by roughly three quarters.

Turning that into a business took Boulton's capital and John Wilkinson's cannon-boring machine, which could bore a cylinder round enough for a piston to seal against. Watt added double action, the sun-and-planet gear to produce rotary motion, a centrifugal governor to hold the speed steady, and the parallel motion linkage he was proudest of. Boulton and Watt charged royalties calculated on the fuel their engines saved, and defended the patent aggressively; its extension to 1800 is often said to have delayed rival designs, particularly high-pressure engines.

Rotary steam power freed factories from rivers, drained deeper mines, and drove the mills, forges, locomotives and ships of the following century. The SI unit of power is named after him, and horsepower was his own marketing comparison against a mill horse.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Watt_steam_engine).

name: Declaration of Independence
summary: The Continental Congress adopted the Declaration of Independence on 4 July 1776, announcing that the thirteen colonies were free and independent states. Its second paragraph, asserting that all men are created equal and hold unalienable rights, became the most quoted statement of the American founding.
body:
Part of [American Revolution](event:american-revolution). Congress voted for independence on 2 July, on a resolution moved by Richard Henry Lee, and approved the wording two days later. Thomas Jefferson wrote the draft in about two weeks; Franklin and Adams suggested changes, and Congress cut roughly a quarter of it, including a passage blaming George III for the slave trade that delegates from South Carolina and Georgia would not accept.

Most of the text is a list of grievances against the king, framed to show a deliberate design to establish tyranny. That was necessary rather than rhetorical: the argument was that the colonies were entitled to dissolve their allegiance, and eighteenth-century readers expected such a case to be made in legal form. The philosophical preamble drew on Locke and on the Virginia Declaration of Rights written weeks earlier by George Mason.

Its claim of equality stood beside the enslavement of about a fifth of the population, and Jefferson himself held people in bondage. Abolitionists, Lincoln at Gettysburg, the Seneca Falls convention of 1848 and the civil rights movement all appealed to the same sentence, which is why it has been called a promissory note. The document was also a diplomatic instrument: independent states could make treaties, and the alliance with France followed.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Declaration_of_Independence).

name: Tay Son Rebellion in Vietnam
summary: The Tay Son brothers led a rebellion from the Vietnamese highlands that overthrew both ruling families, repelled Siamese and Qing invasions, and briefly united the country. The movement fractured after 1792 and was defeated in 1802 by Nguyen Anh, who founded the Nguyen dynasty.
body:
Vietnam had been divided for two centuries between the Trinh lords in the north and the Nguyen in the south, both governing in the name of a powerless Le emperor. Three brothers from the village of Tay Son rose in 1771 against Nguyen taxation, took the southern capital, and by 1786 had destroyed both houses. They redistributed confiscated land, cancelled debts, and recruited officials on ability rather than birth.

Nguyen Hue, the ablest brother, destroyed a Siamese fleet and army at Rach Gam–Xoai Mut in 1785, and in the first days of 1789 marched north and routed a large Qing army at Ngoc Hoi–Dong Da during the lunar new year — the victory best remembered in Vietnam. He took the throne as the Quang Trung emperor and began reforms of the currency, the land registers and the examinations, promoting the vernacular *nom* script in place of classical Chinese.

He died in 1792 at about forty, and the movement split among his heirs. Nguyen Anh, a survivor of the destroyed southern house, rebuilt his forces in the far south with French advisers and arms obtained through the missionary Pigneau de Béhaine, and took Hue and Hanoi in 1802. As the Gia Long emperor he ruled a unified country under the name Vietnam.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tây_Sơn_dynasty).

name: Siege of Yorktown
summary: A combined American and French army trapped Lord Cornwallis's British force on the Virginia peninsula at Yorktown while a French fleet held off relief by sea. Cornwallis surrendered about 7,000 men on 19 October 1781, effectively ending the fighting in America.
body:
Part of [American Revolution](event:american-revolution). Cornwallis had marched north from the Carolinas, where a campaign of small actions had worn his army down, and was ordered to fortify a deep-water port. Washington had been planning to attack New York; on learning that Admiral de Grasse was bringing the French West Indies fleet to the Chesapeake, he marched his own army and Rochambeau's some 700 kilometres south, leaving campfires burning to disguise the move.

The decisive engagement was naval. De Grasse fought off the British relief fleet at the Battle of the Chesapeake on 5 September, after which Cornwallis could be neither reinforced nor taken off. The siege opened on 28 September; French engineers dug the approach trenches, and on 14 October assaults carried redoubts 9 and 10, one of them led by Alexander Hamilton, which let the second parallel reach the river. With his works collapsing under bombardment and a night crossing broken up by a storm, Cornwallis asked for terms.

The garrison marched out to lay down its arms, Cornwallis pleading illness and sending a deputy. News of the surrender brought down Lord North's government in London in March 1782 and opened the negotiations that produced the Treaty of Paris in 1783. Fighting went on elsewhere — the West Indies, Gibraltar, India — but not in the thirteen states.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Yorktown).

name: Chakri Dynasty founded in Siam
summary: General Chao Phraya Chakri took the Siamese throne in 1782 as Rama I, founded the dynasty that still reigns in Thailand, and moved the capital across the river to Bangkok.
body:
The old Siamese capital of Ayutthaya had been destroyed by a Burmese army in 1767. King Taksin drove the Burmese out and rebuilt the kingdom over the following fifteen years from a new capital at Thonburi; in 1782, amid a revolt and reports that the king had become unstable, Taksin was deposed and executed, and his leading general was invited to take the throne.

Rama I moved the seat of government to the east bank at Bangkok and built a walled royal city with the Grand Palace and the temple of the Emerald Buddha, deliberately modelled on the lost Ayutthaya. He had the law recodified in the Three Seals Code, convened a council to revise the Buddhist canon, and rebuilt the administration and army, which held off further Burmese invasions.

His successors met European expansion by conceding what they had to and reforming quickly: Mongkut and Chulalongkorn opened trade, abolished slavery by stages, built railways and telegraphs and centralised the provinces, ceding border territories to Britain and France to keep the core. Siam was the only state in Southeast Asia never colonised. Absolute monarchy ended in a coup in 1932, and the dynasty has continued through wars, constitutions and repeated coups since.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chakri_Dynasty).

name: United States Constitution
summary: Delegates meeting at Philadelphia in the summer of 1787 wrote a constitution replacing the Articles of Confederation with a federal government of three branches. Ratified in 1788 and in force from 1789, it is the oldest written national constitution still operating.
body:
Part of [American Revolution](event:american-revolution). The confederation could not levy taxes or regulate trade, and Shays's Rebellion in Massachusetts in 1786–87 persuaded many that it could not keep order either. The convention was called to amend it and wrote a new instrument instead, sitting behind closed doors through a hot summer with Washington presiding and James Madison taking the notes that are the main record of what was said.

The design was a set of compromises. Large and small states were reconciled by a House apportioned by population and a Senate with two seats each. Slavery was accommodated: enslaved people counted as three-fifths of a person for representation, the slave trade was protected from prohibition until 1808, and escapees had to be returned — none of it named in the text, which avoids the word. Powers were separated and set against one another along lines drawn from [Montesquieu](event:montesquieu-spirit), with an executive chosen by an electoral college rather than by Congress or by voters directly.

Ratification was contested state by state and was argued out in the *Federalist Papers*; several states ratified on the understanding that a bill of rights would follow, and the first ten amendments were adopted in 1791. Judicial review was asserted by the Supreme Court in 1803 rather than written in. The document has been amended twenty-seven times and has been the model for most written constitutions since.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_the_United_States).

name: French Revolution
summary: The French Revolution began in 1789 with a fiscal crisis that became the collapse of the old regime. In ten years France abolished feudal privilege and the monarchy, executed its king, fought most of Europe, killed thousands of its own citizens in the Terror, and ended under a general who made himself ruler.
body:
The crown was bankrupt, partly from the [American war](event:american-revolution), and could not raise taxes without the consent of the privileged orders. The Estates-General met in May 1789 for the first time since 1614; the third estate declared itself a National Assembly, and the [storming of the Bastille](event:bastille) in July, together with a rural panic that summer, forced the abolition of feudal dues and the [Declaration of the Rights of Man](event:rights-of-man).

The constitutional monarchy of 1791 failed. The king's attempted flight destroyed what trust in him remained; war with Austria and Prussia from April 1792 turned every political question into a question of treason; and the monarchy fell in August. Louis XVI was executed in January 1793. Facing invasion, civil war in the Vendée and bread riots, the Convention delegated emergency power to the Committee of Public Safety, and the [Terror](event:terror) that followed executed some 17,000 people by sentence and killed many more in the provinces and in prison. Robespierre fell in July 1794.

The Directory that governed from 1795 balanced between royalists and Jacobins, annulled elections it disliked, and leaned increasingly on an army that was winning in Italy and Germany. In November 1799 [Bonaparte](item:napoleon-bonaparte) [overthrew it](event:napoleon-coup). What the revolution left was durable: legal equality, the end of seigneurial and clerical privilege, the metric system, a civil code, conscription and the nation in arms — and a political vocabulary of left and right, citizen, terror, reaction and ideology that has been in use ever since.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Revolution).

steps.name: The Estates-General and the National Assembly
steps.page:
The Estates-General met at Versailles on 5 May 1789 for the first time since 1614, to solve a fiscal crisis nobody else could. It deadlocked at once over whether the three orders should vote separately, which would let clergy and nobility outvote everyone else.

On 17 June the third estate declared itself a National Assembly with the right to speak for the nation. Locked out of its hall three days later, it gathered in an indoor tennis court and swore not to disperse until France had a constitution.

steps.name: Declaration of the Rights of Man
The flight to Varennes
steps.page:
The royal family slipped out of the Tuileries on the night of 20 June 1791 in a conspicuous coach, heading for loyal troops on the eastern frontier, and were recognised and stopped at Varennes.

Louis had left behind a letter denouncing everything he had agreed to. Brought back through silent crowds, he was suspended and then restored, and signed the constitution in September — but the idea of a king who could be trusted with one had gone.

steps.name: War, the fall of the monarchy and the republic
steps.page:
France declared war on Austria in April 1792 and lost the opening campaign. A manifesto threatening Paris with destruction if the king were harmed produced the opposite: on 10 August a crowd and the Paris sections stormed the Tuileries and the monarchy fell.

Prisoners were massacred in September amid panic about invasion; the army held at Valmy on 20 September; the Convention proclaimed a republic the next day. Louis was tried by it as an ordinary citizen and guillotined on 21 January 1793.

steps.name: Thermidor and the Directory
steps.page:
With Robespierre dead the emergency machinery was dismantled, price controls went, and a harsh winter and inflation fell on the poor of Paris, whose risings were now put down by the army.

The constitution of 1795 set up a five-man Directory and two councils. It survived by annulling elections that went against it, from either side, and depended increasingly on generals — most conspicuously on the young commander of the army of Italy.

name: Storming of the Bastille
summary: On 14 July 1789 a Parisian crowd attacked the Bastille, a royal fortress and prison in the east of the city, and took it after several hours' fighting. It became the symbol of the revolution, and the date is France's national holiday.
body:
Part of [French Revolution](event:french-revolution). The city was tense: bread was dear after a bad harvest, royal troops had been massed around Paris, and on 11 July the king dismissed Necker, the popular finance minister. Crowds seized some 30,000 muskets from the Invalides on the morning of the 14th and went on to the Bastille for the gunpowder stored there.

The fortress mounted guns on its towers and held a garrison of about eighty invalides and thirty Swiss — and seven prisoners: four forgers, two men held as lunatics, and a nobleman. Negotiations broke down, the crowd got into the outer courtyard and cut the drawbridge chains, and firing began; about a hundred attackers were killed. Mutinous royal guards arriving with cannon settled it. The governor, de Launay, surrendered and was killed on the way to the Hôtel de Ville, and his head was carried through the streets on a pike.

The Bastille had long stood for imprisonment by royal warrant without trial, which is why its fall meant far more than its garrison or its prisoners did. It was demolished within months and its stones sold as souvenirs. Told of it that night, the king asked whether it was a revolt; it is a revolution, he was told.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Storming_of_the_Bastille).

name: Declaration of the Rights of Man
summary: The National Assembly adopted the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen on 26 August 1789. Its seventeen articles state that men are born free and equal in rights, that sovereignty belongs to the nation, and that law is the expression of the general will.
body:
Part of [French Revolution](event:french-revolution). It was drafted in the weeks after the [Bastille](event:bastille) and the August abolition of feudal privileges, with Lafayette among its authors and advice from Jefferson, then American minister in Paris. It drew on the American declarations and on [Rousseau](event:rousseau-social) and [Montesquieu](event:montesquieu-spirit), and was intended as the preamble to a constitution not yet written.

The articles name liberty, property, security and resistance to oppression as natural rights; require that arrest, punishment and taxation rest on published law; guarantee the presumption of innocence and freedom of opinion and of the press; and demand that public officials account for their administration. Liberty is defined as the freedom to do anything that does not harm another, with limits set only by law.

Its silences were disputed at once. Women were not included, and Olympe de Gouges answered with a *Declaration of the Rights of Woman* in 1791; she was guillotined in 1793. Colonial slavery was not addressed, a gap the [Haitian Revolution](event:haitian-revolution) closed in its own way. The text is still part of French constitutional law and stands behind the Universal Declaration of Human Rights of 1948.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Declaration_of_the_Rights_of_Man_and_of_the_Citizen).

name: Haitian Revolution
summary: Enslaved people in the French colony of Saint-Domingue rose in 1791 and, after thirteen years of war against French, Spanish and British forces, founded the independent state of Haiti on 1 January 1804. It is the only slave revolt in history that produced a state.
body:
Saint-Domingue was the most profitable colony in the world, producing about two-fifths of the sugar and half the coffee consumed in Europe with the labour of some half a million enslaved people, most of them African-born under a mortality regime that required constant replacement. The [French Revolution](event:french-revolution) split the free population over who was entitled to its rights, and in August 1791 the enslaved people of the northern plain rose and burned the plantations.

The revolt survived because it exploited a war among empires. Toussaint Louverture, a former coachman freed before the revolution, fought first for Spain and then for France once the republic abolished slavery in 1794, and drove out both the Spanish and a British expedition that lost tens of thousands of men to yellow fever. By 1801 he governed the whole island and issued a constitution making himself governor for life.

Napoleon sent his brother-in-law Leclerc with a large expedition in 1802 to restore French control and, where it had been abolished, slavery. Toussaint was seized under a flag of truce and died in a prison in the Jura; when the intention to reimpose slavery became plain, his generals resumed the war. Disease destroyed the French army, and Jean-Jacques Dessalines won the last battle at Vertières in November 1803. Haiti was then isolated by slaveholding powers for decades, and in 1825 agreed to pay France an indemnity for the lost property — including the people — a debt that burdened its finances into the twentieth century.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haitian_Revolution).

steps.name: The rising in the north
steps.page:
A ceremony at Bois Caïman, led by the houngan Dutty Boukman, is remembered as the signal for the revolt. On the night of 21 August 1791 the enslaved population of the northern plain rose, and within weeks over a thousand plantations had been burned.

The colonial militia and free coloured planters could not contain it. What began as a rising against particular masters became an army with commanders, camps and diplomacy.

steps.name: Emancipation in the colony and in France
steps.page:
With Spain and Britain invading and the colony slipping away, the republican commissioner Sonthonax proclaimed the abolition of slavery in the northern province on 29 August 1793, to win the insurgents to the French side.

The National Convention in Paris ratified and extended it on 4 February 1794, abolishing slavery in all French colonies. Toussaint Louverture, who had been fighting for Spain, changed sides within months.

steps.name: Toussaint drives out the Spanish and the British
steps.page:
Toussaint pushed the Spanish out of the east, and by 1795 Spain had ceded its half of the island to France. The British expedition that had landed in 1793 to seize the richest colony in the Caribbean was worn down by ambush and by yellow fever.

It withdrew in October 1798 having lost tens of thousands of men, most of them to disease, and having agreed terms directly with Toussaint.

steps.name: Toussaint governs, and the constitution of 1801
steps.page:
Toussaint defeated his rival André Rigaud, occupied the Spanish east of the island, and by 1801 governed it all. He tried to restart the sugar economy with paid but compulsory plantation labour, which was unpopular with the people who had fought.

The constitution he promulgated in July 1801 abolished slavery for ever, made him governor for life with the right to name his successor, and left France a nominal sovereignty. Napoleon read it as a declaration of independence.

steps.name: The Leclerc expedition
steps.page:
Napoleon sent his brother-in-law Leclerc with the largest force France had ever sent overseas — some 30,000 men — to restore direct rule and, where it had been abolished, slavery. Cap-Français was burned rather than surrendered.

Toussaint fought, negotiated, and was seized under a flag of truce in June and deported to the Fort de Joux in the Jura, where he died the following April. Yellow fever then destroyed the French army, Leclerc among them, and news that slavery had been restored in Guadeloupe brought his own black officers back into the war.

steps.name: Vertières
steps.page:
Jean-Jacques Dessalines united the surviving commanders under a flag made by tearing the white out of the French tricolour. The last French field force was beaten at Vertières, outside Cap-Français, on 18 November 1803.

Rochambeau, who had waged the final campaign with mass drownings and imported war dogs, capitulated days later and surrendered to a British blockading squadron.

steps.name: Independence declared
steps.page:
At Gonaïves on 1 January 1804 Dessalines proclaimed independence and restored the island's Taíno name, Haiti. It was the second independent state in the Americas and the first anywhere founded by former slaves.

France did not recognise it until 1825, and then in return for an indemnity of 150 million francs; the United States withheld recognition until 1862. Isolation and the debt shaped Haitian history for a century and more.

name: The Reign of Terror
summary: The Reign of Terror was the period from September 1793 to July 1794 in which the French revolutionary government used mass arrest and summary trial against suspected enemies. About 17,000 people were executed by sentence, and many more died in prison or in the suppression of revolt.
body:
Part of [French Revolution](event:french-revolution). It followed a summer of emergencies: foreign armies on French soil, a royalist and Catholic rising in the Vendée, revolt in Lyon and Toulon, food shortages, and the assassination of Marat. The Convention concentrated executive power in the Committee of Public Safety, of which Robespierre became the best-known member, and declared terror "the order of the day" on 5 September 1793.

The Law of Suspects allowed the arrest of anyone whose conduct, connections or writings suggested hostility to the revolution. The Revolutionary Tribunal in Paris tried in batches, and the Law of 22 Prairial in June 1794 removed defence counsel and left it only acquittal or death. Marie Antoinette, the Girondin deputies, Danton and finally Robespierre's own allies went to the guillotine in turn. The worst violence was in the provinces: mass shootings at Lyon, drownings at Nantes, and a campaign in the Vendée that killed far more than the Paris tribunal ever did.

It went with a war economy that worked: price controls, requisition, and a levy that put over 700,000 men in the field and turned the invasions back. As the emergency eased the justification thinned, and on 9 Thermidor — 27 July 1794 — the Convention turned on Robespierre, who was executed the next day. It has been argued over ever since as either the price of the republic's survival or the pattern of what revolutionary government becomes.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reign_of_Terror).

name: Jenner's smallpox vaccine
summary: In May 1796 Edward Jenner, a country doctor in Gloucestershire, inoculated a boy with matter from a cowpox sore and then exposed him to smallpox; the boy did not take the disease. The method, which he called vaccination, was the first reasonably safe protection against smallpox.
body:
Smallpox killed an estimated 400,000 Europeans a year in the eighteenth century and blinded or disfigured many who survived. The existing defence was variolation — deliberate infection with smallpox itself, long practised in China, India and the Ottoman world and introduced to Britain in the 1720s by Lady Mary Wortley Montagu — which conferred immunity but killed one or two in a hundred and could start an outbreak.

That dairymaids who had had cowpox seemed to be spared was folk knowledge, and at least one farmer, Benjamin Jesty, had acted on it twenty years earlier. What Jenner did was test it and publish. He inoculated James Phipps, aged eight, with material from a sore on the hand of the dairymaid Sarah Nelmes, challenged him with smallpox some weeks later, repeated the procedure on others, and published the results in 1798 at his own expense. *Vaccine* comes from *vacca*, cow.

Vaccination spread within a few years across Europe and the Americas — a Spanish expedition carried it to the empire in 1803 in a chain of orphan children — and was made compulsory in several countries during the nineteenth century, against organised resistance. A global campaign led by the World Health Organization from 1967 [eradicated smallpox](event:smallpox-eradication); the last natural case was in 1977. It remains the only human disease deliberately eliminated.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smallpox_vaccine).

name: Napoleon seizes power
summary: On 9 and 10 November 1799 — 18 and 19 Brumaire in the revolutionary calendar — Napoleon Bonaparte and a group of conspirators overthrew the Directory and set up a Consulate with himself as First Consul. It is the conventional end of the French Revolution.
body:
Part of [French Revolution](event:french-revolution). The plot was not originally his. Emmanuel Sieyès, one of the five Directors, wanted a stronger executive and was looking for a general to supply the force; [Bonaparte](item:napoleon-bonaparte), who had abandoned his army in Egypt and come home to a hero's reception, was not the first choice but was the one who profited.

The councils were moved out to Saint-Cloud on the pretext of a Jacobin conspiracy, and Bonaparte was given command of the troops in Paris. His speech to the deputies on the second day went badly — he was shouted down and jostled, and there were calls to declare him an outlaw — and it was his brother Lucien, presiding over the lower council, who saved the coup by telling the grenadiers outside that the assembly was being held at daggerpoint. Soldiers cleared the hall, and a rump voted the Directory out that evening.

The constitution that followed vested executive power in three consuls and, in practice, in the first of them. Bonaparte made peace with the church, codified the civil law and centralised the administration through appointed prefects. He was made consul for life in 1802 and Emperor of the French in 1804.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coup_of_18_Brumaire).
